Measure Less, Know More:
Self-Supervised Test-Time Feature Acquisition

Eeshaan Jain Affiliation: School of Computer and Communication Sciences, EPFL Email: eeshaan.jain@epfl.ch    Linus Bleistein Affiliation: School of Computer and Communication Sciences, EPFL Affiliation: School of Life Sciences, EPFL Email: linus.bleistein@epfl.ch    Bart Deplancke Affiliation: School of Life Sciences, EPFL Email: bart.deplancke@epfl.ch    Charlotte Bunne Affiliation: School of Computer and Communication Sciences, EPFL Affiliation: School of Life Sciences, EPFL Email: charlotte.bunne@epfl.ch
Abstract

Recent progress in multimodal, high-dimensional learning has enabled foundation models to process heterogeneous, large-scale data. However, at test time, acquiring all features or modalities can be prohibitively costly and often redundant. Sequentially selecting informative modalities is therefore critical, yet challenging when the downstream task or prediction target is unknown. To this end, we introduce echo-kk, a task-agnostic and self-supervised learning principle for modality acquisition: we use a deep model’s internal pretrained representations (e.g., from a foundation model) as proxy targets that summarize cross-modal information. We provide theoretical guarantees in a stylized linear setting that motivate a reinforcement learning (RL) policy for sequential modality selection. Across task-agnostic and label-free acquisition baselines, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k consistently improves budgeted downstream performance across diverse foundation-model backends. Our method provides a principled route to cost-aware test-time deployment, with implications for any multimodal system where measurements are expensive or time-constrained, and downstream tasks unknown a priori. The code is available at  github.com/bunnelab/echo-k.

1 Introduction

Multimodal foundation models (FMs) thrive on more information: the more modalities we can feed them at test time, the more accurate, robust, and context-aware their representations become (Kaplan et al., 2020; Zhai et al., 2022; Mizrahi et al., 2023; Shukor et al., 2025). In practice, however, not every modality is available by default. Each additional assay, sensor, or data source carries a tangible cost in time, money, throughput, or patient burden. This creates a deployment gap: while models can theoretically produce rich representations by exploiting multiview data, acquiring all views for every instance is infeasible.

Modalities are stratified by cost, latency, and availability: in clinical diagnostics, routine measurements are often available immediately, while additional molecular or imaging assays can disambiguate uncertain cases but are constrained by turnaround time, cost, or limited sample material. Similar asymmetries arise in scientific discovery, where inexpensive proxies can be collected at scale, but high-fidelity measurements require specialized instrumentation or scarce experimental time. Measurements are therefore not acquired exhaustively, nor independently, but as structured groups of modalities or features corresponding to coherent sensing processes. We refer to each such group as a view. Under a fixed budget, only a small number of views can be queried per instance, and the value of each view depends on which views have already been observed. The acquisition problem is therefore inherently sequential and adaptive: at test time, given the views observed so far, which view should a foundation model acquire next to most improve its downstream predictions?

Existing approaches to sequential acquisition are typically task- and data-driven: they define utility with respect to a specific downstream objective, such as classification or regression, and optimize expected task loss  (Gong et al., 2019; Gadgil et al., 2023; Guney et al., 2025). This paradigm requires labeled data at acquisition time, task-specific reward design, or explicit modeling of task uncertainty. As a result, acquisition policies are tightly coupled to a particular task and dataset, and must be retrained or redesigned when downstream objectives change. This reliance on supervision has left the fully task-agnostic, label-free acquisition setting largely unaddressed (see Related Work in § B). Yet modern pretrained models are increasingly deployed as frozen backbones whose representations support many downstream tasks. This shift suggests a different perspective on acquisition: rather than selecting measurements for a single supervised objective, one can ask which measurements are needed to preserve the representation formed by the pretrained model.

In this work, we propose to use these latent representations learned by modern foundation models as a task-agnostic signal for view acquisition. When trained on heterogeneous, multiview data, these models learn compressed representations that integrate complementary evidence across views into a compact state (Radford et al., 2021; Siméoni et al., 2025; Wenckstern et al., 2025; Oquab et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2024; Qu et al., 2025; Shmatko et al., 2025). This latent state encodes the information the model deems relevant across many downstream tasks. We use these rich latent states as a learning objective: rather than defining utility with respect to a specific downstream objective, we learn a view selection policy that iteratively selects views to approximate the full latent representation from a minimal number of views.

Learning acquisition policies in representation spaces has two main advantages. On the one hand, it removes dependence on downstream supervision: acquisition decisions can be learned without task labels or task-specific losses. On the other hand, it enables broad transfer: because the representation is shared across tasks, preserving it supports many downstream objectives simultaneously. If the partial-view representation closely matches the full-view representation, then any downstream predictor operating on that representation should incur minimal degradation, independent of the task.

We instantiate this principle with echo-kk, a reinforcement learning algorithm for long-horizon sequential view acquisition that modularly integrates with any self-supervised (foundation) model (Fig. 1). At each step, the RL agent selects which view to acquire next and the reward quantifies progress toward the corresponding full-view representation. Once trained, the policy is deployed at inference time on unobserved views to allocate acquisition budgets on an instance-by-instance basis.

We support this algorithm with the first theoretical analysis of self-supervised feature acquisition: in a linear model, where we show that representation recovery controls the latent representation regret (Theorem 3.5), and that conditioning on partial observations yields provable gains over fixed orderings. These results in turn justify the RL reward design and motivate the long-horizon acquisition strategy, enabling cost-effective deployment of large multimodal models in settings where full multiview acquisition is impractical.

Contributions. Our contributions are as follows.

  1. 1.

    We introduce a model-driven framework for self-supervised feature acquisition, in which acquisition decisions are guided by the internal representations of pretrained models, without access to task-specific supervision.

  2. 2.

    We provide the first theoretical analysis of self-supervised feature acquisition. In a stylized linear setting, we derive performance bounds that relate optimal test-time policies and oracle selection strategies, formally characterizing the gap induced by limited information that motivate an RL-based acquisition strategy.

  3. 3.

    We develop echo-kk, a cost-efficient reinforcement learning algorithm that learns long-horizon acquisition policies using self-supervised latent representations. The policy is trained to maximize progress toward the full-view representation, translating the representation-recovery principle into a practical sequential acquisition method.

  4. 4.

    Empirically, we show that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k learns effective acquisition strategies across diverse data modalities and acquisition horizons. Across image, tabular, single-cell transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, and multimodal geospatial benchmarks, the learned policies rapidly concentrate informative views in early acquisition stages, validating the effectiveness and generality of representation-driven acquisition under realistic budget constraints.

Our contributions bridge theory and practice in unsupervised feature acquisition, enabling foundation models to reason about what to measure next under realistic constraints.

2 Representation-Driven Acquisition as a Markov Decision Process

In the absence of a specified downstream task, acquisition requires a notion of value that is independent of labels. We define this value through the pretrained multiview encoder: acquired views should recover the representation obtained from all views.

Setup. Concretely, we consider nn i.i.d. samples, each with KK possible views 𝒙i=(𝒎1i,…,𝒎Ki)\bm{x}^{i}=(\bm{m}_{1}^{i},\dots,\bm{m}_{K}^{i}) drawn from a joint distribution over the product space of multiple views ℳ1×⋯×ℳK\mathcal{M}^{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{M}^{K}. 11 1 Throughout, we use the term view to represent either a modality or a feature group acquired jointly, as our framework applies uniformly to all such settings. After selection, each view 𝒎k\bm{m}_{k} is processed by a view-specific encoder Φk:ℳk→ℝdk\Phi_{k}:\mathcal{M}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}} 22 2 Note, under this framework, multiple views can also share the same joint encoder, or correspond to unimodal encoders. and combined via a fixed aggregation 𝐀𝐖:ℝd1×…​ℝdK→ℝp\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\times\dots\mathbb{R}^{d_{K}}\to\mathbb{R}^{p} parameterized by 𝐖\mathbf{W}, yielding the full-view representation 𝒛∗=𝐀𝐖​(Φ1​(𝒎1),…,ΦK​(𝒎K))\bm{z}^{*}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}\!\left(\Phi_{1}(\bm{m}_{1}),\dots,\Phi_{K}(\bm{m}_{K})\right). This formulation subsumes both multimodal, where each view corresponds to a distinct sensing modality, and unimodal models in which views are partitioned into acquisition units but processed by a shared encoder. For notational simplicity, we absorb encoders into the views and write 𝒛∗\bm{z}^{*} directly. We let 𝑷t⊆[[1,K]]{\bm{P}}_{t}\subseteq[\![1,K]\!] be the acquired set after tt steps, with induced partial representation 𝒛⁡(𝑷t):=𝐀𝐖​({Φk​(𝒎k):k∈𝑷t})\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t}):=\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}\!\left(\{\Phi_{k}(\bm{m}_{k}):k\in{\bm{P}}_{t}\}\right).

Objective.

We measure acquisition quality through the representation-recovery loss ℒ⁡(𝑷t):=‖𝒛⁡(𝑷t)−𝒛⋆‖22,\mathcal{L}({\bm{P}}_{t}):=\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t})-\bm{z}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}, and seek a sequence (k1,…,kT)(k_{1},\ldots,k_{T}) minimizing ℒ⁡(𝑷T)\mathcal{L}({\bm{P}}_{T}) under budget T≪KT\ll K. The ideal one-step oracle greedy rule is

kt+1∈arg​mink∉𝐏t⁡‖𝐳⁡(𝐏t∪{k})−𝐳∗‖22.k_{t+1}\in\argmin_{k\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}}\left\|\bm{z}\!\left({\bm{P}}_{t}\cup\{k\}\right)-\bm{z}^{*}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (1)
From training to test-time deployment.

The ideal policy defined above is not deployable at test time. Indeed, it requires both the full-view representation 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} and forward passes for every candidate view. During training, we use unlabeled data to construct a self-supervised representation-recovery signal to train a view-selection policy. In the complete-reference setting, fully observed training samples allow us to compute the full-view representation 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} and use it as the reference target. More generally, when only a subset of views Ri⊆[[1,K]]R_{i}\subseteq[\![1,K]\!] is available for training instance ii, we can use the corresponding reference representation 𝒛⁡(Ri)\bm{z}(R_{i}) as a partially observed target. In both cases, downstream labels are not used to train the acquisition policy. At deployment, the learned policy acts solely from the current acquisition state st=(𝑷t,𝒛⁡(𝑷t),bt)s_{t}=({\bm{P}}_{t},\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t}),b_{t}); 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} is never accessed.

Downstream tasks.

A representation-recovery objective is only meaningful if minimizing it translates to better performance on downstream tasks. If gg is an LgL_{g}-Lipschitz downstream predictor and the loss ℓ\ell is LℓL_{\ell}-Lipschitz in the prediction, then for any acquired set 𝑷{\bm{P}},

ℓ⁡(g⁡(𝒛⁡(𝑷)),y)−ℓ⁡(g⁡(𝒛∗),y)≤Lℓ​Lg​‖𝒛⁡(𝑷)−𝒛∗‖2.\ell\!\left(g(\bm{z}({\bm{P}})),\,y\right)-\ell\!\left(g(\bm{z}^{*}),\,y\right)\;\leq\;L_{\ell}L_{g}\,\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}})-\bm{z}^{*}\|_{2}.

This provides a simple sufficient condition under which latent recovery bounds the degradation of a fixed downstream predictor. In our experiments, downstream labels are not used to train the acquisition policy; they are used only post hoc to evaluate whether the recovered representations preserve task-relevant information.

The training-deployment asymmetry shown above raises the central theoretical question: how much is lost when acquisition proceeds from partial observations, relative to an oracle greedy policy that can evaluate the full-information value of each view? A complete MDP formulation is given in § C.

3 Theoretical Guarantees

To quantify the cost of this partial observability, we compare two idealized strategies in a stylized linear setting: (i) an oracle policy that observes the full view vector 𝒙\bm{x} and greedily selects the view that most reduces representation error, and (ii) an optimal test-time policy that makes the same greedy choice but conditions only on previously acquired views. The gap between such oracle and limited-information strategies has been studied in supervised settings (He et al., 2012; Madasu et al., 2022; Valancius et al., 2023); our contribution is to characterize it in the self-supervised, representation-recovery setting, where no task labels are available.

Let 𝒙∈ℝd\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} be a random view vector and 𝒛∗=𝒛⁡(𝒙):=𝐖​𝒙∈ℝm\bm{z}^{*}=\bm{z}(\bm{x}):=\mathbf{W}\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{m} a latent representation where 𝐖=(𝐰i​k)∈ℝm×d\mathbf{W}=(\mathbf{w}_{ik})\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times d} is a fixed linear aggregation operator. This setting captures the last-layer behavior of linear or locally linearized representation models. Policies iteratively construct a view subset 𝑷t⊆[[1,d]]{\bm{P}}_{t}\subseteq[\![1,d]\!]; at step tt, the quality of the selected set 𝑷t{\bm{P}}_{t} is measured by the conditional expected square reconstruction error

ℒ⁡(𝑷t∣ℐt)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}({\bm{P}}_{t}\mid\mathcal{I}_{t}) :=∑i=1m𝔼⁡[(∑k=1d𝐰i​k​xk−∑k∈𝑷t𝐰i​k​xk)2|ℐt]=∑i=1m𝔼⁡[(∑k∉𝑷t𝐰i​k​xk)2|ℐt],\displaystyle:=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Big(\sum_{k=1}^{d}\mathbf{w}_{ik}x_{k}-\sum_{k\in{\bm{P}}_{t}}\mathbf{w}_{ik}x_{k}\Big)^{2}\Big|\;\mathcal{I}_{t}\right]=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\mathbb{E}\!\left[\Big(\sum_{k\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}}\mathbf{w}_{ik}x_{k}\Big)^{2}\Big|\;\mathcal{I}_{t}\right],

where ℐt\mathcal{I}_{t} denotes the information available to the policy at time tt, which is different for each policy.

One-step oracle policy.

The one-step oracle policy greedily selects views with full access to the realization of 𝒙\bm{x}. Given a set 𝑷t⋆\bm{P}_{t}^{\star} selected at time tt, the oracle chooses

kt⋆\displaystyle k_{t}^{\star} ∈arg​mink∉𝐏t⋆∑i=1m(∑j∉𝐏t⋆∪{k}𝐰ijxj)2=arg​mink∉𝐏t⋆∑j∉𝐏t∗∪{k}‖𝐰j‖22​xj2⏟=:𝐄j+∑j≠j′j,j′∉𝐏t∗∪{k}𝐰j⊤​𝐰j′​xj​xj′⏟=:𝐂jj′,\displaystyle\in\argmin_{k\notin\bm{P}_{t}^{\star}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\Bigg(\sum_{j\notin\bm{P}_{t}^{\star}\cup\{k\}}\mathbf{w}_{ij}x_{j}\Bigg)^{2}=\argmin_{k\notin\bm{P}_{t}^{\star}}\sum_{j\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}^{*}\cup\{k\}}\underbrace{\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}x_{j}^{2}}_{=:\bm{E}_{j}}+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\neq j^{\prime}\\ j,j^{\prime}\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}*\cup\{k\}\end{subarray}}\underbrace{\mathbf{w}_{j}^{\top}\mathbf{w}_{j^{\prime}}x_{j}x_{j^{\prime}}}_{=:\bm{C}_{jj^{\prime}}},

where 𝐰k\mathbf{w}_{k} denotes the kk-th column of 𝐖\mathbf{W}. The oracle therefore exploits both individual view contributions 𝑬k\bm{E}_{k} (energies) and cross-view interaction terms Ck​k′C_{kk^{\prime}}, made possible by full knowledge of 𝒙\bm{x}. A test-time policy, by contrast, cannot evaluate the Ck​k′C_{kk^{\prime}} terms, since they depend on the unobserved views; it must instead rely on conditional expectations given observed views.

Test-time policies.

We define the class of one-step test-time policies as stochastic mappings that, at each step, select a new view based solely on the history of previously observed views and update their beliefs over the unobserved ones. Formally, such policies are adapted to the filtration ℱt:=σ(xk:k∈𝑷t)\mathcal{F}_{t}:=\sigma(x_{k}:k\in{\bm{P}}_{t}) and therefore operate under partial observability, in contrast to the oracle. Among this class, the optimal test-time policy greedily minimizes the conditional expected representation loss, with perfect knowledge of the conditional distribution of unobserved views given observed ones. Given the current selected set 𝑷^t\widehat{\bm{P}}_{t}, this policy chooses

k^t∈arg​mink∉𝐏^t⁡[∑j∉𝐏^t∪{k}𝔼⁡[𝐄j|ℱt]+∑j≠j′j,j′∉𝐏^t∪{k}𝔼⁡[𝐂jj′|ℱt]],\displaystyle\widehat{k}_{t}\in\argmin_{k\notin\widehat{{\bm{P}}}_{t}}\Bigg[\sum_{j\notin\widehat{{\bm{P}}}_{t}\cup\{k\}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{E}_{j}|\mathcal{F}_{t}]+\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}j\neq j^{\prime}\\ j,j^{\prime}\notin\widehat{{\bm{P}}}_{t}\cup\{k\}\end{subarray}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{C}_{jj^{\prime}}|\mathcal{F}_{t}]\Bigg],

where 𝑬j\bm{E}_{j} and 𝑪j​j′\bm{C}_{jj^{\prime}} are as defined in the oracle decomposition. To quantify performance, we define the true loss incurred after selecting 𝑷t{\bm{P}}_{t} as ℒ⁡(𝑷t,𝒙):=‖∑k∉𝑷t𝐰k​xk‖22\mathcal{L}({\bm{P}}_{t},\bm{x}):=\left\|\sum_{k\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}}\mathbf{w}_{k}x_{k}\right\|_{2}^{2}, and the latent regret of the test-time policy as ℛt:=𝔼𝒙​[ℒ⁡(𝑷^t,𝒙)]−𝔼𝒙​[ℒ⁡(𝑷t⋆,𝒙)],\mathcal{R}_{t}:=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\Big[\mathcal{L}(\widehat{\bm{P}}_{t},\bm{x})\Big]-\mathbb{E}_{\bm{x}}\Big[\mathcal{L}(\bm{P}^{\star}_{t},\bm{x})\Big], where 𝑷t⋆\bm{P}_{t}^{\star} denotes the view set selected by the oracle after tt steps.

Proxy loss.

The true loss includes pairwise interaction terms 𝑪j​j′\bm{C}_{jj^{\prime}}, so the marginal value of a view depends on the entire set of unobserved views; thus bounding expected regret would require controlling the distribution of orderings in a quadratically coupled system, which is analytically intractable without additional structure. To isolate the effect of partial observability from this combinatorial difficulty, we analyze a proxy objective ℒ~​(𝑷t,𝒙):=∑k∉Pt𝔼⁡[𝑬k∣ℐt]\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{P}_{t},\bm{x}):=\sum_{k\notin P_{t}}\mathbb{E}[\bm{E}_{k}\mid\mathcal{I}_{t}] and connect it back to the true regret in Theorem 3.5. Two quantities govern the proxy analysis: the centered variables 𝒀j,s:=𝑬j−𝔼⁡[𝑬j|ℱs]\bm{Y}_{j,s}:=\bm{E}_{j}-\mathbb{E}[\bm{E}_{j}|\mathcal{F}_{s}] measure how far each view’s energy deviates from its conditional expectation at step ss, and the maximal conditional deviation 𝑹s:=maxi,j∉𝑷^t⁡(Yi,s−Yj,s)\bm{R}_{s}:=\max_{i,j\notin\widehat{{\bm{P}}}_{t}}(Y_{i,s}-Y_{j,s}) captures the worst-case spread of these estimation errors among unselected views.

3.1 Pathwise Decomposition of the Proxy Regret

We now study the gap between the one-step oracle policy and the optimal test-time policy under the proxy objective. Lemma 3.1 provides a pathwise bound on their difference.

Lemma 3.1.

For all t≥2t\geq 2, the proxy loss gap satisfies

ℒ~(𝑷^t,𝒙)−ℒ~(𝑷t⋆,𝒙)≤∑s=1t𝟏{k^s∈Bt}𝑹s,\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(\widehat{\bm{P}}_{t},\bm{x})-\widetilde{\mathcal{L}}(\bm{P}^{\star}_{t},\bm{x})\leq\sum\limits_{s=1}^{t}\bm{1}_{\{\widehat{k}_{s}\in B_{t}\}}\bm{R}_{s}, (2)

where BtB_{t} denotes the mismatch set between the oracle and test-time selections up to time tt.

Lemma 3.1 reduces the proxy regret to a sum of weighted mistake events: regret is incurred only when the test-time policy selects a view outside the oracle-selected set, and the magnitude of each mistake is controlled by the conditional deviation 𝑹s\bm{R}_{s}.

Crucially, extending this bound beyond a pathwise statement requires detailed control over the distribution of the order statistics of (𝑬k)k=1d(\bm{E}_{k})_{k=1}^{d}. In particular, bounding the expected regret entails enumerating all possible orderings of the view energies and characterizing the frequencies and magnitude of deviation of the two policies. Without structural assumptions on the joint distribution of (𝑬k)(\bm{E}_{k}), we find such a control to be intractable.We therefore posit a latent-variable model in which the data is driven by a shared discrete factor with Gumbel noise, which induces a tractable Plackett–Luce distribution over view rankings (Yellott Jr, 1977; Ma et al., 2021) and makes the regret analysis possible.

Assumption 3.2 (Gumbel latent correlation model).

The view vector 𝐱∈ℝd\bm{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is strictly positive and satisfies log⁡𝐱=𝛈+𝛃⊙Z+ε,\log\bm{x}=\bm{\eta}+\bm{\beta}\odot Z+\varepsilon, where 𝛈,𝛃∈ℝd\bm{\eta},\bm{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} are deterministic, and the common latent factor ZZ is a discrete latent variable taking values in z1,…,zM{z_{1},\dots,z_{M}} with probabilities p1,…,pM{p_{1},\dots,p_{M}}. The noise terms follow εj​∼i.i.d.​Gumbel​(0,σ)\varepsilon_{j}\overset{\mathrm{i.i.d.}}{\sim}\mathrm{Gumbel}(0,\sigma) with σ∈(0,1/4)\sigma\in(0,1/4). We further assume that for all latent states zmz_{m}, ℙ⁡[Z=zm∣ℱs]>0\mathbb{P}[Z=z_{m}\mid\mathcal{F}_{s}]>0.

Under Assumption 3.2, the conditional ordering of the energies (𝑬j)j=1d(\bm{E}_{j})_{j=1}^{d} given Z=zmZ=z_{m} follows a Plackett–Luce distribution. Specifically, for any permutation π\pi of 1,…,d{1,\dots,d},

ℙ⁡(𝑬π⁡(1)≥⋯≥𝑬π⁡(d)∣Z=zm)=∏s=1dehπ⁡(s),zm∑r=sdehπ⁡(r),zm,\displaystyle\mathbb{P}\Big(\bm{E}_{\pi(1)}\geq\dots\geq\bm{E}_{\pi(d)}\mid Z=z_{m}\Big)=\prod\limits_{s=1}^{d}\frac{e^{h_{\pi(s),z_{m}}}}{\sum\limits_{r=s}^{d}e^{h_{\pi(r),z_{m}}}},

where (hj,zm)j,m(h_{j,z_{m}})_{j,m} are model-dependent utilities determined by (𝜼,𝜷,σ)(\bm{\eta},\bm{\beta},\sigma). Marginally, the induced ranking distribution is therefore a mixture of Plackett–Luce models over the latent states of ZZ. The role of the Gumbel assumption is not primarily to model the data distribution itself, but to ensure that the ranking of view energies follows a tractable parametric family, which is what makes the regret analysis possible. Fig. 5 provides visualizations of datasets generated under this model.

3.2 Regret Bounds under the Gumbel Model

For each latent state mm, define the utilities uj(m):=2​log⁡(‖𝐰j‖2)+2​ηj+2​βj​zmu_{j}^{(m)}:=2\log(\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2})+2\eta_{j}+2\beta_{j}z_{m} and let γ:=minm∈[M]⁡minj≠j′​|uj(m)−uj′(m)|>0\gamma:=\min_{m\in[M]}\min_{j\neq j^{\prime}}\left|u_{j}^{(m)}-u_{j^{\prime}}^{(m)}\right|>0 denote the minimum separation between utilities. A larger γ\gamma allows easier identification of view-energy rankings. Also, denote pmin=minm=1,…,M⁡pmp_{\min}=\min_{m=1,\dots,M}p_{m}.

A key step is to bound the number of disagreements between the oracle and optimal test-time policies. Let GtG_{t} (resp. BtB_{t}) denote the set of views selected only by the oracle (resp. optimal test-time) policy at time tt, and define

Rmax:=maxj∈[d]⁡maxm⁡e2​βj​zmminm⁡e2​βj​zm<∞, and ​εγ:=eγ−1Rmax+eγ−1∈(0,1).R_{\max}:=\max_{j\in[d]}\frac{\max_{m}e^{2\beta_{j}z_{m}}}{\min_{m}e^{2\beta_{j}z_{m}}}<\infty,\text{ and }\varepsilon_{\gamma}:=\frac{e^{\gamma}-1}{R_{\max}+e^{\gamma}-1}\in(0,1).
Lemma 3.3.

The expected number of oracle-test-time mismatches satisfies, for any λ>0\lambda>0,

𝔼​|Bt|=𝔼​|Gt|≤Dt​(λ):=min⁡{t,d−t,Cλ1−ρλ+1eρ∗−1}\mathbb{E}|B_{t}|=\mathbb{E}|G_{t}|\leq D_{t}(\lambda):=\min\left\{t,d-t,\frac{C_{\lambda}}{1-\rho_{\lambda}}+\frac{1}{e^{\rho_{*}}-1}\right\} (3)

where Cλ:=(M−1)​(1−εγεγ​pmin)λC_{\lambda}:=(M-1)\left(\frac{1-\varepsilon_{\gamma}}{\varepsilon_{\gamma}p_{\text{min}}}\right)^{\lambda}, ρ⋆:=1−e−γ/(2σ)\rho_{\star}:=1-e^{-\gamma/(2\sigma)}, and ρλ\rho_{\lambda} is a contraction constant (see § F.4).

Proof outline.

The analysis proceeds in three steps: (i) we bound the number of oracle–test-time disagreements (ii) this yields a proxy regret bound via the pathwise decomposition; (iii) we relate proxy and true losses through a structural assumption on the embedding weights. For proofs, see § E.

The regret on the proxy controls errors due to partial observability, but says nothing about the gap between the proxy and true losses. Bridging this gap requires a condition on the geometry of the embedding weights: if the normalized columns of 𝐖\mathbf{W} are approximately orthogonal, the cross-view interaction terms 𝑪j​j′\bm{C}_{jj^{\prime}}, that the proxy ignores, remain small.

Assumption 3.4 (Near Isometry).

There exists constants CC, peff>0p_{\textnormal{eff}}>0 such that for any subset J⊆{1,…,d}J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\} of size mm, the matrix 𝐁J=(𝐰u/‖𝐰u‖)u∈J\bm{B}_{J}=\big(\mathbf{w}_{u}/\left\|\mathbf{w}_{u}\right\|\big)_{u\in J} satisfies

‖𝑩J⊤​𝑩J−𝑰m‖op≤C⁡(mpeff+mpeff).\displaystyle\left\|\bm{B}_{J}^{\top}\bm{B}_{J}-\bm{I}_{m}\right\|_{\textnormal{op}}\leq C\Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{m}{p_{\textnormal{eff}}}}+\frac{m}{p_{\textnormal{eff}}}\Bigg).

This condition enforces approximate orthogonality of embedding directions and is empirically satisfied by large-scale vision transformers such as the DINOv2 family (Oquab et al., 2023) and by trained autoencoders across a range of dimensions (§ H.9.2). It ensures that the cross-view interaction terms ignored by the proxy objective remain controlled, so that the proxy loss remains aligned with the true latent reconstruction loss. We can now state the main result.

Theorem 3.5.

Take p∈(1,12​σ)p\in\big(1,\frac{1}{2\sigma}\big) and let q=pp−1q=\frac{p}{p-1}. Under Assumptions 3.2 and 3.4, for any λ>0\lambda>0, the latent regret satisfies

ℛt≤\displaystyle\mathcal{R}_{t}\leq (∑i=1dM(i)​min⁡(t,d−i+1))1/p​Dt1/q+C′​(Ntpeff+Ntpeff)​Dt​Nt,\displaystyle\left(\sum_{i=1}^{d}M_{(i)}\min(t,d-i+1)\right)^{1/p}D_{t}^{1/q}+C^{\prime}\Bigg(\sqrt{\frac{N_{t}}{p_{\textnormal{eff}}}}+\frac{N_{t}}{p_{\textnormal{eff}}}\Bigg)\sqrt{D_{t}N_{t}}, (4)

where Mj:=𝔼⁡[𝐄jp]M_{j}:=\mathbb{E}[\bm{E}_{j}^{p}] and M(1)≥⋯≥M(d)M_{(1)}\geq\cdots\geq M_{(d)} be the sorted pp-th moments, and Nt=d−t+DtN_{t}=d-t+D_{t}.

The bound separates two sources of error. The first term is an oracle-mismatch term: it captures the cost of partial observability through the disagreement envelope DtD_{t}. This term decreases as the utility gap γ\gamma increases, reflecting that well-separated energy rankings are easier to infer from partial observations. The second term is a spectral misalignment term: it controls the error introduced by replacing the true latent loss with the marginal-energy proxy. Consequently, the bound is boundary-correct: since Dt=0D_{t}=0 at t=0t=0 and t=dt=d, both terms vanish at the endpoints, matching the reverse-U regret profile observed empirically in Fig. 2.

4 Methodology

4.1 From Theoretical Test-Time Policies to Learnable Policies

The theoretical analysis in § 3 yields three insights that directly inform algorithm design. First, Theorem 3.5 shows that representation-recovery errors control latent regret up to an oracle-mismatch term and a spectral misalignment term, which becomes small when embedding directions are approximately orthogonal. This motivates using progress toward the full-view representation as a self-supervised acquisition signal. Second, the posterior concentration result (Lemma F.4) shows that conditioning on observed views can reduce the gap to a full-information oracle, motivating adaptive, instance-specific policies that update after each acquisition. Third, the analysis is restricted to myopic policies: the oracle itself is one-step greedy, and the regret bound characterizes the gap between two greedy strategies. In practice, the conditional law of unobserved views given ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} is unknown, and acquisition is a finite-horizon decision problem in which early choices affect the value of later measurements, especially when views are correlated (Shim et al., 2018; Zannone et al., 2019; Kachuee et al., 2019; Schütz et al., 2025). This motivates moving beyond the greedy regime to long-horizon planning.

Together, these insights culminate in echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, a reinforcement-learning algorithm for self-supervised, long-horizon view acquisition. We use the theory to define a reward, and learn a parameterized policy that optimizes cumulative improvement in representation quality over an entire acquisition trajectory, rather than approximating the one-step oracle. Formally, we aim to learn a parameterized policy π^𝜽\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}} that maximizes cumulative discounted improvement starting from any step ss

max⁡∑t=sd𝜽∈𝚯⁡αt−s​𝔼​[Rt​(π𝜽​(𝑷t−1))],\displaystyle\max\limits_{\bm{\theta}\in\bm{\Theta}}\,\,\sum\limits_{t=s}^{d}\alpha^{t-s}\mathbb{E}\big[R_{t}\Big(\pi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{P}_{t-1})\big)\Big],

where RtR_{t} denotes the incremental improvement in latent representation quality at step tt, α∈(0,1]\alpha\in(0,1] is a discount factor that allows the policy to trade off immediate gains against future benefits. The self-supervised reward requires a reference representation against which partial representations are compared. We consider two training regimes. In the complete-reference setting, each training instance is fully observed, so the reference is the full-view representation 𝒛i⋆=𝒛i​([[1,K]])\bm{z}_{i}^{\star}=\bm{z}_{i}([\![1,K]\!]). In the partially observed-reference setting, training instance ii contains only a subset of available views Ri⊆[[1,K]]R_{i}\subseteq[\![1,K]\!]; in this case, we use 𝒛iref=𝒛i​(Ri)\bm{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}=\bm{z}_{i}(R_{i}) as a noisy but label-free reference target.

4.2 Learning Representation-Driven Policies

Reward.

Given the reference representation 𝒛iref\bm{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}, we define the representation error for instance ii as ℓi​(S):=‖𝒛iref−𝒛i​(S)‖2\ell_{i}(S):=\|\bm{z}_{i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-\bm{z}_{i}(S)\|_{2}. The step-wise reward is the normalized improvement in the error,

Rt​(π^𝜽):=ωt​1N​∑i=1Nℓi​(𝑷t−1i)−ℓi​(𝑷t−1i∪{kti})ℓi​(∅)+ϵ,R_{t}(\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}}):=\omega_{t}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{\ell_{i}({\bm{P}}_{t-1}^{i})-\ell_{i}({\bm{P}}_{t-1}^{i}\cup\{k_{t}^{i}\})}{\ell_{i}(\varnothing)+\epsilon}, (5)

where NN is the minibatch size, and kti∼π^𝜽(⋅∣st−1i)k_{t}^{i}\sim\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1}^{i}) is the view selected for instance ii at step tt. We use the unsquared norm rather than the squared loss analyzed in § 3, as this provides more stable reward scaling in practice. The reward 5 retains the same structure as the representation-recovery objective studied theoretically: it measures marginal progress toward a reference latent representation without using downstream labels. The factor ωt\omega_{t} optionally upweights early acquisition steps, where marginal gains are typically largest, and normalization prevents high-error instances from dominating the learning signal. Moreover, when views have nonuniform acquisition costs ckc_{k}, we use a cost-aware reward of the form rtcost=rt−λc​1N​∑i=1Ncktir_{t}^{\mathrm{cost}}=r_{t}-\lambda_{c}\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}c_{k_{t}^{i}} with costs normalized across views.

Policy input.

At each step, the policy receives the current partial representation 𝒛i​(𝑷ti)\bm{z}_{i}({\bm{P}}_{t}^{i}), the observed view values with unobserved entries masked, the acquisition mask, and the remaining budget. In heterogeneous-cost experiments, the state is additionally augmented with the view-cost vector and remaining cost budget; the full state specification is given in § G.5.

Optimization.

We optimize π^𝜽\widehat{\pi}_{\bm{\theta}} using Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017), with invalid action masking (Huang and Ontañón, 2020) to prevent re-selection of already acquired views. During both training and deployment, the policy has access only to the frozen representation model and partial observations induced by the current acquisition set.

5 Experimental Results

We evaluate echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k across controlled synthetic experiments, vision, and tabular encoders, and three frozen foundation-model settings: single-cell transcriptomics with TABULA (Ding et al., 2025), spatial proteomics with VirTues (Wenckstern et al., 2025), and multimodal geospatial sensing with a self-supervised multimodal encoder (Gordon et al., 2026). The experiments are designed to answer four questions: (i) whether representation-driven acquisition improves downstream performance under limited budgets; (ii) whether the same label-free acquisition principle composes with heterogeneous pretrained backbones; (iii) whether learned acquisition policies transfer to downstream tasks unseen during policy learning; and (iv) whether the method remains effective under realistic deployment constraints, including partially observed reference data and heterogeneous acquisition costs. We discuss the results for foundation models, grouped by application domain, here. Additional controlled benchmarks on synthetic data, and vision datasets such as MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and MiniBooNE, a physics benchmark, along with incorporating costs and adaptive stopping, are shown in § H.

Evaluation.

Across all experiments, the representation model is frozen and receives partially observed inputs. echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k learns an acquisition policy using only self-supervised rewards derived from progress toward a reference latent representation. In the complete-reference setting, this reference is the full-view embedding; in the partially observed-reference setting, it is computed from the subset of views available for each training instance. Downstream labels are never used for policy learning and are reserved exclusively for post-hoc evaluation. At deployment, the policy observes only the values of the views acquired so far and the acquisition mask, and never accesses the full-view representation or downstream labels. To measure downstream performance, we train a single linear probe per downstream task on partial embeddings using random masking augmentation, and keep it fixed across acquisition budgets. The same probe is applied to the partial embeddings induced by every acquisition method, so that differences in performance reflect only which views were acquired. Moreover, a single acquisition policy is learned per backbone and reused across all budgets and downstream tasks, including tasks that were not specified during policy learning. All results are averaged over three random seeds (§ G.3).

Baselines and metrics.

We compare against 12 baselines spanning oracle/random references, model-driven heuristics (GIR, ESM2-based orderings), and unsupervised feature selection methods (Laplacian Score, spec-φ3\varphi_{3}, MCFS, UDFS, SVD-Ent, Variance) adapted as acquisition orders (see § G.4 for details). The Oracle greedily selects the view that maximally reduces the distance to the full-view embedding using unobserved values; it is not deployable at test time and serves as an upper bound on greedy acquisition. Domain-specific baselines are evaluated only where they are defined, e.g., ESM2-based orderings require protein-sequence embeddings and are therefore restricted to protein markers. Since most of these baselines induce a fixed, instance-independent acquisition order, we additionally compare against label-free instance-adaptive policies (§ 5.3) and supervised acquisition methods that use downstream labels (§ H.4). For regression, we report R2R^{2} or MSE, and for other real-world tasks, classification accuracy as a function of the acquisition budget t∈[[1,d]]t\in[\![1,d]\!], reported as a fraction of the total number of views. To directly assess the training objective, we further report the normalized representation recovery (§ 5.4). For full evaluation details, refer to § G.

5.1 Evaluation on Foundation Model Backends

Single-cell foundation models.

In single-cell RNA-seq, selecting the right genes is a critical bottleneck, and the same panel must often support multiple analyses such as cell type annotation, trajectory inference, or gene program discovery that may not be specified at design time (Fig. 3a). We pair echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with TABULA (Ding et al., 2025), a FM for single-cell transcriptomics (§ G.2).

Results. We evaluate on hPancreas, a curated single-cell transcriptomics (RNA-seq) collection from human pancreatic tissue (Ding et al., 2025), retaining the top 200 highly variable genes across 14 cell types. We use cell type annotation as a representative downstream task; it is the standard evaluation objective in single-cell analysis and requires the gene subset to preserve fine-grained phenotypic distinctions (§ G.1). echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k underperforms slightly during the first ∼\sim2–3% of acquisitions but rapidly recovers and consistently outperforms Variance, GIR, and Random thereafter (Fig. 3b). Random performs poorly throughout, reflecting the sparsity of informative genes in high-dimensional expression data.

Spatial proteomics foundation models.

In spatial proteomics, multiplexed protein imaging characterizes tissue through successive rounds of antibody staining, each revealing a new marker and adding to assay cost, imaging time, and tissue degradation risk. Panel design must therefore support multiple diagnostic objectives simultaneously (e.g., cancer subtyping and grading), with different patients potentially benefiting from different markers (Fig. 4a). We compose echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with the VirTues foundation model (Wenckstern et al., 2025), which embeds multiplex imaging data into tissue-level representations. At deployment, the policy mirrors the iterative staining workflow: selecting which marker to acquire next, updating its partial representation, and using the updated embedding to inform the next selection (§ G.5).

Results. We evaluate on a non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) patient cohort (Cords et al., 2024) profiled by imaging mass cytometry with 40 protein markers spanning tumor, immune, stromal, and vascular compartments. We consider two clinically relevant downstream tasks: cancer subtyping (2 classes) and cancer grading (3 classes), the latter being substantially more challenging (§ G.1). echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k consistently outperforms baselines on both tasks (Figs. 4b,c). The scatter plot in Fig. 4d shows that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k achieves favorable accuracy on both tasks under identical acquisition orders, demonstrating task-agnostic panel design. A qualitative analysis (§ H.10) reveals that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k prioritizes clinically established markers such as panCK, Ki-67, and CD4 early in the process, consistent with domain knowledge (Martin et al., 2004; Su et al., 2006), despite receiving no supervision. Acquisition orders differ substantially across samples, with mean pairwise Kendall’s τ=0.06\tau=0.06. Across training seeds, orders for the same sample show greater agreement: mean τ=0.512\tau=0.512 and 61.6% top-five overlap, compared with 12.8% under random ordering.

Multimodal geospatial foundation models.

Earth observation integrates heterogeneous sensing products, from optical and radar imagery to terrain, land-cover, canopy-height, meteorological, and geolocation-derived variables. We evaluate echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k on MMEarth-Bench (Gordon et al., 2026), a globally distributed benchmark of 12 aligned geospatial modalities, treating each modality as a separately acquirable view.

Results. We evaluate on soil pH regression as an unseen downstream task, reporting R2R^{2} as a function of the number of modalities. echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k outperforms non-oracle baselines consistently under limited modality budgets, reaching strong predictive performance after acquiring only 20-30% of the views (Fig. 3b). We also notice that GIR and Variance-based baselines are the second-best performers.

5.2 Robustness to Partially Observed Reference Data

In Table 1, we evaluate whether echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k remains effective when trained from incomplete views by randomly masking a fraction mm of views before computing the reference embedding, and train the policy against this partially observed target. For single-cell transcriptomics FMs, performance is nearly unchanged for m=m=10%, remains strong for m=m=20%, and still recovers high accuracy under heavier missingness once moderate acquisition budgets are allowed. For proteomics FMs, performance degrades more gradually with mm, but partially observed-reference policies remain competitive with strong baselines across budgets. We also notice that for high budgets, GIR is competitive with echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k. Overall, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k degrades smoothly rather than collapsing, suggesting that useful acquisition policies can be learned from incomplete reference representations.

5.3 Comparison with Adaptive Acquisition

Beyond fixed acquisition orderings, we compare echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with label-free, instance-adaptive policies under the same information setting: GSMRL-AIR (Li and Oliva, 2021), based on conditional generative imputations; Adaptive Latent Gain (ALG), which predicts one-step representation gain; and Cluster Information Gain (CIG), which estimates view-wise information gain under a Gaussian mixture model. echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k outperforms all three across every budget on MiniBooNE (Table 2) and hPancreas (§H.3). Notably, ALG shares echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k ’s state and reward but optimizes only one-step gain, highlighting the benefit of long-horizon acquisition. Finally, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k remains competitive with supervised acquisition policies that have access to downstream labels (§ H.4), quantifying the cost of task agnosticism.

5.4 Comparison of representation-recovery

While our main results focus on downstream performance, we also directly evaluate the representation-recovery objective optimized by echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k (Eq. 5). For each instance ii, we define normalized recovery after tt acquisitions as

ρi,t:=1−‖𝒛i​(𝑷ti)−𝒛i⋆‖2‖𝒛i​(∅)−𝒛i⋆‖2,\rho_{i,t}:=1-\frac{\|\bm{z}_{i}({\bm{P}}_{t}^{i})-\bm{z}_{i}^{\star}\|_{2}}{\|\bm{z}_{i}(\varnothing)-\bm{z}_{i}^{\star}\|_{2}},

We report ρt\rho_{t} averaged over test instances. Table 3 shows that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k achieves higher recovery than Variance, the strongest competing baseline on both hPancreas and MiniBooNE, across all budgets. Moreover, recovery and downstream accuracy exhibit the same ordering (Fig. 3b; Fig. 7): better preservation of the full-view representation corresponds to better downstream performance. This provides empirical support for the connection established in Theorem 3.5 between representation recovery and downstream error.

6 Conclusion

We presented echo-kk, a task-agnostic and label-free framework for sequential test-time view acquisition that uses a pretrained model’s latent representation as a self-supervised proxy: under a cost budget, acquire views so that the induced partial representation rapidly approaches the full-view representation. We support this formulation with a theoretical analysis in a linear setting that characterizes the gap between oracle and feasible test-time policies, and we introduce a practical cost-aware RL algorithm that learns long-horizon acquisition strategies. Experiments with controlled synthetic data and multimodal foundation models across single-cell transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, and geospatial sensing show improved budgeted acquisition, provide evidence for transfer to downstream tasks unseen during policy learning, robustness to partially observed reference data, and extensibility to heterogeneous acquisition costs. The broader implication is that foundation models need not remain passive predictors over pre-collected inputs; they can become resource-aware systems that actively shape the evidence available for inference.

Appendix

Appendix A Impact and Limitations

echo-kk enables multimodal representation models to operate under test-time measurement budgets by learning task-agnostic, label-free acquisition policies. Instead of requiring downstream labels to decide which view to acquire next, the method uses the model’s own full-view representation as a self-supervised reference. This addresses a practical deployment bottleneck: multimodal and scientific foundation models often benefit from additional inputs, but acquiring all modalities can be infeasible due to cost, latency, limited tissue or sample material, scarce instrumentation time, or experimental constraints. In scientific settings, echo-kk could help prioritize which measurements, assays, markers, sensors, or experiments to run next under limited resources. In clinical settings, it could support budget-aware acquisition of follow-up tests or multimodal patient measurements, while keeping downstream decision-making within validated and expert-supervised workflows. The main limitations concern deployment specificity rather than the general formulation. Acquisition costs and constraints may vary across domains, so practical use requires defining the relevant budget, availability, and cost model for the target setting. The method also benefits from reference representations that are informative enough to guide policy learning; our robustness experiments suggest that these references need not always be complete, but the appropriate level of missingness may depend on the application and backbone. Finally, as with any method intended for scientific or clinical use, policies should be evaluated on the intended endpoint and deployment distribution before adoption. Moreover, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k preserves whatever information the pretrained backbone encodes, and does not assert that the full-view representation 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} is optimal for every downstream task; any task-irrelevant information in 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} is therefore inherited from the backbone. Our experiments evaluate transfer across downstream objectives, but do not test explicit distribution shift between the reference-construction data and the deployment domain. Similarly, the full-view representation is not always the best training target: masked references outperform it on MNIST-14 at 20% and 40% budgets and on hPancreas at 20% (§ H), suggesting that masking can act as a mild regularizer during training. Our robustness sweep considers randomly masked reference views and does not identify where partial references fail, since even at 50% masking echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k remains competitive with strong baselines. A natural extension is structured incompleteness, where an entire assay or modality is missing for a subset of samples, and understanding how the reference representation interacts with that structure is an interesting direction for future work. These considerations leave substantial room for future work on richer cost models, uncertainty-aware acquisition, and prospective validation in real-world acquisition workflows.

Appendix B Related Work

Classical feature selection methods aim to find a subset of relevant features that maximizes model performance while excluding irrelevancies (Kohavi and John, 1997; Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003). Early surveys (Blum and Langley, 1997) reviewed both empirical advances and theoretical definitions of feature relevance, formalizing the notions of strong and weak relevance. Several works cast the problem as submodular optimization (Killamsetty et al., 2021; Jain et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2014; Coleman et al., 2019), though their end goal is to improve performance under limited budget during training rather than at test time. Previous work has also centered around greedy heuristics with theoretical guarantees for sequential search (Golovin and Krause, 2011). Another line of work focuses on instance-specific or personalized feature selection (Melville et al., 2004; Li et al., 2018). Beyond selecting a subset of features, a related field is feature importance quantification: given a fixed dataset and (most commonly) a target, the goal is to isolate features that contribute significantly to predictions (Guyon and Elisseeff, 2003; Settles, 2009; Li et al., 2017; Lundberg and Lee, 2017; Sristi et al., 2023; Jain et al., 2023; Lifshitz et al., 2025). Model-specific methods such as (Breiman, 2001) leverage the structure of the model to assign importance ranks, while model-agnostic methods (Fisher et al., 2019) rely on importance metrics applicable to any model.

Active learning (AL) incorporates a sample selection policy in the training loop in an online fashion: at each time tt, a new sample is queried to augment the existing dataset (Settles, 2009; Zhan et al., 2022; Tharwat and Schenck, 2023; Li et al., 2025). AL methods are particularly well suited for settings where acquiring new samples is expensive. They can be broadly split into three types of strategies (Zhan et al., 2022). Uncertainty-based querying strategies select points based on the estimated information they provide to the learning algorithm, including maximum entropy selection (Shannon, 1948), confidence-based selection (Wang and Shang, 2014), and adversarial methods (Ducoffe and Precioso, 2018). Diversity-based strategies aim to increase the coverage of samples in the dataset, for instance through core-set approaches that build subsets approximating the full dataset (Sener and Savarese, 2017; Claici et al., 2018; Feldman, 2019; Kim and Shin, 2022). Lastly, combined strategies mix both approaches (Yin et al., 2017; Zhdanov, 2019; Shui et al., 2020).

Feature acquisition (FA). Our method focuses on designing instance-specific feature acquisition strategies rather than sample acquisition policies (Settles, 2009; Kirsch et al., 2019; Holzmüller et al., 2023; Kolossov et al., 2023; Gupte et al., 2024). FA strategies can be broadly split (Rahbar et al., 2025) into greedy strategies that sequentially acquire information by maximizing expected utility, and non-greedy methods that plan acquisition over multiple time steps (Zubek and Dietterich, 2002; Dulac-Arnold et al., 2011; Shim et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2018; Huang et al., 2025; Norcliffe et al., 2025; Piskorz et al., 2025), often using reinforcement learning (Shim et al., 2018; Zannone et al., 2019; Kachuee et al., 2019). This problem has also been studied under the name of Bayesian experiment design (BED), which aims to optimize the distribution of ξ\xi, the random variable controlling the experiment, in order to maximize the information gain obtained by running the experiment parametrized by ξ\xi (Chaloner and Verdinelli, 1995; Sebastiani and Wynn, 2000; Cavagnaro et al., 2010; Ryan et al., 2016; Rainforth et al., 2024). Classical BED methods sequentially update a model from a stream of incoming experiments; recently, the focus has shifted towards policy learning (Foster et al., 2021; Blau et al., 2022; Blau et al., 2023) and decision-aware experiment design (Huang et al., 2024).

Task-agnostic acquisition. Contrarily to previous work, our proposed method is fundamentally task-agnostic. While some active learning and feature selection strategies have considered weakly or unlabeled settings (Ash et al., 2019; Yehuda et al., 2022; Lifshitz et al., 2025; Kobayashi et al., 2025), task-agnostic feature acquisition has received little attention. Closest to our setup are Li and Oliva (2021), who consider a partially supervised setup and tackle this problem by training a surrogate reward model, and introduce an active instance recognition task in which the goal is to select features to reduce uncertainty.

Theoretical aspects of FA have received little attention, both in the supervised and unsupervised setting. Chen et al. (2015) study a probabilistic model inspired by Bayesian experiment design, in which the goal is to learn a policy that sequentially acquires features to infer the value of a target. Kobayashi et al. (2025) and Covert et al. (2023) provide theoretical insights in the supervised case. Our work is the first to consider the unsupervised case and to provide a bound on the gap between the greedy oracle and the optimal test-time policy.

Appendix C Extended Mathematical Framework

Data generation.

We consider nn i.i.d. instances. For each i∈[[1,n]]i\in[\![1,n]\!], the data 𝒙i=(𝒎1i,…,𝒎Ki)\bm{x}^{i}=(\bm{m}_{1}^{i},\dots,\bm{m}_{K}^{i}) is drawn from a joint distribution over ℳ1×⋯×ℳK\mathcal{M}^{1}\times\cdots\times\mathcal{M}^{K}. We use view, modality, and feature group interchangeably, as our framework applies uniformly to all settings.

Representation model.

Each view 𝒎k\bm{m}_{k} is processed by a view-specific encoder Φk:ℳk→ℝdk\Phi_{k}:\mathcal{M}^{k}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{k}}. The encoded views are combined through a fixed aggregation function 𝐀𝐖:ℝd1×⋯×ℝdK→ℝp\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}:\mathbb{R}^{d_{1}}\times\dots\times\mathbb{R}^{d_{K}}\to\mathbb{R}^{p}, yielding the full-view representation 𝒛∗=𝐀𝐖​(Φ1​(𝒎1),…,ΦK​(𝒎K))\bm{z}^{*}=\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}\!\left(\Phi_{1}(\bm{m}_{1}),\dots,\Phi_{K}(\bm{m}_{K})\right). This subsumes both multimodal models (each 𝒎k\bm{m}_{k} is a distinct modality: image, audio, protein marker, …) and unimodal models (features partitioned into jointly acquired groups processed by a shared encoder). For notational simplicity, we drop the encoders in subsequent expressions and treat views as directly mapped into the latent space.

Sequential acquisition.

Let 𝑷t⊆[[1,K]]{\bm{P}}_{t}\subseteq[\![1,K]\!] denote the acquired set after tt steps and 𝒛⁡(𝑷t):=𝐀𝐖​({Φk​(𝒎k):k∈𝑷t})\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t}):=\mathbf{A}_{\mathbf{W}}\!\left(\{\Phi_{k}(\bm{m}_{k}):k\in{\bm{P}}_{t}\}\right) the induced partial representation, with unobserved views treated as missing. The finite-horizon acquisition problem is to select a sequence (k1,…,kT)(k_{1},\ldots,k_{T}), with kt+1∉𝑷tk_{t+1}\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}, minimizing the representation-recovery loss

ℒ⁡(𝑷t):=‖𝒛⁡(𝑷t)−𝒛⋆‖22.\mathcal{L}({\bm{P}}_{t}):=\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t})-\bm{z}^{\star}\|_{2}^{2}.

Equivalently, the policy maximizes cumulative progress toward 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} along the acquisition trajectory. The ideal one-step greedy rule is

kt+1∈arg​mink∉𝐏t⁡‖𝐳⁡(𝐏t∪{k})−𝐳∗‖22,k_{t+1}\in\argmin_{k\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}}\left\|\bm{z}\!\left({\bm{P}}_{t}\cup\{k\}\right)-\bm{z}^{*}\right\|_{2}^{2}, (6)

which is not deployable at test time, since it requires access to both 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} and the representation after acquiring each candidate view.

Markov decision process formulation.

We frame sequential acquisition as an instance-specific MDP with a continuous state space and evolving action set. Dropping the instance superscript for clarity, the components are:

  • •

    State. At step tt, the state is st=(Mt,𝒙𝑷t,𝒛⁡(𝑷t),bt)s_{t}=(M_{t},\bm{x}_{{\bm{P}}_{t}},\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t}),b_{t}), where Mt∈{0,1}KM_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{K} is the acquisition mask, 𝒙𝑷t\bm{x}_{{\bm{P}}_{t}} are the observed view values, 𝒛⁡(𝑷t)\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t}) is the current partial representation, and btb_{t} is the remaining budget. To maintain a fixed state space across steps, unobserved views are set to NA, so the augmented space is (ℳ1∪{NA})×⋯×(ℳK∪{NA})\big(\mathcal{M}^{1}\cup\{\texttt{NA}\}\big)\times\cdots\times\big(\mathcal{M}^{K}\cup\{\texttt{NA}\}\big) (Norcliffe et al., 2025).

  • •

    Actions. The available actions at step tt are the unacquired views: 𝒜⁡(st)={k∈[[1,K]]:k∉𝑷t}\mathcal{A}(s_{t})=\{k\in[\![1,K]\!]:k\notin{\bm{P}}_{t}\}.

  • •

    Transitions. Upon selecting kt+1k_{t+1}, its value is drawn from 𝒎kt+1∼pdata(⋅∣𝒎k,k∈𝑷t)\bm{m}_{k_{t+1}}\sim p_{\texttt{data}}(\cdot\mid\bm{m}_{k},k\in{\bm{P}}_{t}), the state updates to 𝑷t+1=𝑷t∪{kt+1}{\bm{P}}_{t+1}={\bm{P}}_{t}\cup\{k_{t+1}\}, and 𝒛⁡(𝑷t+1)\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t+1}) is recomputed. The transition probability between states differing only in coordinate ktk_{t} is

    ℙ⁡[𝑷t∣𝑷t−1]=ℙ⁡[at=kt∣𝑷t−1]⋅pdata​(𝒎kt∣𝒎k,k∈𝑷t−1).\mathbb{P}\!\left[{\bm{P}}_{t}\mid{\bm{P}}_{t-1}\right]=\mathbb{P}\!\left[a_{t}=k_{t}\mid{\bm{P}}_{t-1}\right]\cdot p_{\texttt{data}}\!\left(\bm{m}_{k_{t}}\mid\bm{m}_{k},\,k\in{\bm{P}}_{t-1}\right).
  • •

    Reward. The reward at step t+1t+1 quantifies progress toward the reference-view representation:

    rt+1​(𝑷t+1):=‖𝒛⁡(𝑷t)−𝒛ref‖22−‖𝒛⁡(𝑷t+1)−𝒛ref‖22.r_{t+1}({\bm{P}}_{t+1}):=\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t})-\bm{z}^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}-\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t+1})-\bm{z}^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{2}^{2}.

    where 𝒛ref\bm{z}^{\mathrm{ref}} can be the full view embedding 𝒛∗\bm{z}^{*} or the embedding from all the views (can be a subset of full views) measured for the underlying data point.

Selection policies.

A stochastic selection policy is a map πθ(⋅∣st)∈Δ(𝒜(st))\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t})\in\Delta(\mathcal{A}(s_{t})), where Δ⁡(𝒜⁡(st))\Delta(\mathcal{A}(s_{t})) is the probability simplex over available actions. During training, fully observed samples allow 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} to be computed and used as a self-supervised target — no downstream labels are required. When only a reference subset RiR_{i} is observed for instance ii, 𝒛⁡(Ri)\bm{z}(R_{i}) serves as a partial target. At deployment, the learned policy is fixed and acts solely from the current state sts_{t}.

Connection to sequential decision making.

This MDP is an instance of a KK-armed bandit with correlated arms and a single-pull constraint per arm (Gupta et al., 2021); see also Guha and Munagala (2007); Chakrabarti et al. (2008); Carrara et al. (2019) for related setups. The sequential decision problem is Markovian with respect to (𝑷t,𝒛⁡(𝑷t))({\bm{P}}_{t},\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t})): given the current partial representation and acquired set, future acquisition values are independent of the full history of selections.

Appendix F Technical Lemmas

F.1 Technical Lemma 1: Inclusion of Mismatch Events

Recall that for any subset A⊆{1,…,d}A\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}, rkA​(k)\textsc{rk}_{A}(k) is the rank of 𝑬k\bm{E}_{k} among all (𝑬j)j∈A(\bm{E}_{j})_{j\in A}. Consider the event

Bad(s,t):={rk𝑷^−s(k^s+1)>t−s}={𝑬k^s+1<𝑬(t−s)}.\displaystyle\textsc{Bad}(s,t):=\big\{\textsc{rk}_{\widehat{\bm{P}}_{-s}}(\widehat{k}_{s+1})>t-s\big\}=\Big\{\bm{E}_{\widehat{k}_{s+1}}<\bm{E}_{(t-s)}\Big\}.
Lemma F.1.

We have

∑s=2t𝟏{k^s∈Bt}𝑹s≤∑s=2t𝟏Bad​(s,t)𝑹s.\displaystyle\sum\limits_{s=2}^{t}\bm{1}_{\{\widehat{k}_{s}\in B_{t}\}}\bm{R}_{s}\leq\sum\limits_{s=2}^{t}\bm{1}_{\textsc{Bad}(s,t)}\bm{R}_{s}.\vskip-10.0pt

Proof. At time s≤ts\leq t, the test-time policy has selected at most s−1s-1 items from the top t−1t-1 values of (𝑬k)k=1d(\bm{E}_{k})_{k=1}^{d}, the most favorable case being when it selects the same items as the oracle policy. Hence, there are at least t−s−1t-s-1 items from the top t−1t-1 values of (𝑬k)k=1d(\bm{E}_{k})_{k=1}^{d} in the set 𝑷^−s\widehat{\bm{P}}_{-s}. Therefore, if k^s∈Bt\widehat{k}_{s}\in B_{t}, then by definition it is not in the top t−s−1t-s-1 items, because it would otherwise also belong to Gt=𝑷t⋆\BtG_{t}=\bm{P}^{\star}_{t}\backslash B_{t}. Hence,

𝑬k^s≤𝑬(t−s−1).\displaystyle\bm{E}_{\widehat{k}_{s}}\leq\bm{E}_{(t-s-1)}.

We have hence proved that {k^s∈Bt}⊆Bad(s,t)\{\widehat{k}_{s}\in B_{t}\}\subseteq\textsc{Bad}(s,t), which proves our claim.

Appendix G Experimental Details

G.1 Datasets

We evaluate echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k and all baselines on six datasets spanning seven downstream tasks. Table 5 provides a summary. Below we describe each dataset in detail, including the downstream task, preprocessing choices, and the specific aspects that make it relevant for evaluating budgeted feature acquisition.

G.1.1 Vision Datasets: MNIST and Fashion-MNIST

MNIST (LeCun et al., 1998) and Fashion-MNIST (Xiao et al., 2017) are standard computer vision benchmarks consisting of images of handwritten digits and Zalando article images, respectively. Both have 10-class classification as the downstream task. Following Li and Oliva (2021), we downsample images from 28×2828\times 28 to 14×1414\times 14 resolution, treating each pixel as an independently acquirable feature and yielding d=196d=196 acquisition units. This downsampling increases the information density per pixel and makes the acquisition problem more challenging, since fewer pixels suffice to reach a given accuracy. We use a 70:15:15 split (50k/10k/10k). To ensure a controlled comparison, all acquisition methods are initialized from the same top-corner pixel (   ), so differences in accuracy reflect only the quality of the subsequent acquisition strategy.

G.1.2 Physics: MiniBooNE

The MiniBooNE dataset (Roe, 2005) originates from the Fermilab MiniBooNE neutrino experiment. The goal is binary classification: distinguishing electron-neutrino signal events from muon-neutrino background events. The dataset contains d=33d=33 reconstructed physics variables derived from detector signals, including Cherenkov ring characteristics, event energy, and track reconstruction outputs. In practice, computing these reconstructed variables from raw detector data is expensive and the variables exhibit substantial mutual correlations, making it undesirable to rely on the full feature set at test time. We adopt the preprocessing protocol of Norcliffe et al. (2025), which standardizes features and removes duplicate events, and use a 70:15:15 split (65k/5k/6k). This dataset is particularly relevant for evaluating echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k because the strong inter-feature correlations create a setting where greedy, myopic acquisition can be suboptimal: selecting the individually most informative variable first may be redundant with the second-most informative one, motivating the long-horizon planning that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k provides.

G.1.3 Single-Cell Transcriptomics: hPancreas

The hPancreas dataset (Ding et al., 2025) is a curated single-cell RNA-sequencing collection from human pancreatic tissue with 14 cell type labels spanning endocrine, exocrine, and immune populations. This dataset is widely used as a benchmark in the single-cell foundation model literature. From the 1,200 genes available, we retain the top 200 most variable genes using Cell Ranger (Zheng et al., 2017) and ScanPy (Wolf et al., 2018), following standard practice for reducing noise from uninformative transcripts while preserving biologically meaningful variation. We use the preprocessing, gene filtering, and data splits provided by (Ding et al., 2025) (9.5k/1k/4.2k). Cell-type annotation serves as a representative downstream task: it is the most common evaluation objective in single-cell analysis and requires the acquired gene subset to preserve fine-grained phenotypic distinctions between closely related cell populations. Crucially, the echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k policy is trained without any access to cell-type labels; the annotation task is used purely for post-hoc evaluation of the acquired gene panels.

G.1.4 Spatial Proteomics: NSCLC Patient Cohort

The NSCLC clinical cohort (Cords et al., 2024) consists of spatial proteomics data acquired via imaging mass cytometry (IMC) at 1​μ​m1\,\mu\mathrm{m}/px resolution with d=40d=40 semantically meaningful protein markers. The marker panel includes tumor markers (e.g., panCK), proliferation markers (e.g., Ki-67), immune cell markers (e.g., CD4, CD8, CD68), stromal markers, and vascular markers, providing a comprehensive view of the tumor microenvironment. Clinical annotations include cancer subtyping (2 classes: adenocarcinoma vs. squamous cell carcinoma) and cancer grading (3 classes), the latter being substantially more challenging due to subtler morphological and molecular differences between grades. We adopt the preprocessing pipeline described in (Wenckstern et al., 2025), which includes cell segmentation, marker normalization, and quality filtering. The experimental setup is inherently sequential: echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k iteratively selects one protein marker at a time, the VirTues backbone updates its tissue embedding given the newly observed marker, and the updated embedding informs the next acquisition decision. This mirrors the real-world workflow in multiplexed imaging, where tissue sections are characterized through successive rounds of antibody staining and each additional round carries a cost. The acquisition budget is set to T=10T=10 markers (25% of the full panel), reflecting realistic constraints on antibody panel size in clinical multiplex imaging.

G.1.5 Geospatial Earth Observations: MMEarth-Bench

The MMEarth-Bench dataset (Gordon et al., 2026) is a global multimodal Earth-observation benchmark to evaluate models under heterogeneous sensing conditions. Each location is represented by 12 aligned geospatial views, including optical satellite imagery, radar measurements, terrain and elevation products, land-cover maps, canopy-height information, meteorological variables, and geolocation metadata. It provides a multimodal acquisition setting: each view corresponds to a distinct sensing product or environmental data source that may differ in availability, cost, spatial resolution, and information content. We treat each modality group as one acquisition unit and pair echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with a frozen multimodal geospatial representation model trained on the full set of available views. We evaluate downstream transfer on soil pH regression, reporting R2R^{2} as a function of the acquired modality budget.

G.1.6 Synthetic Dataset

We generate synthetic data under the data generating process (DGP) of Assumption 3.2. We consider a gradient correlation family shared by a common latent state ZZ, where Z∼Discrete​({zm}m=1M,{pm}m=1M)Z\sim\text{Discrete}\left(\{z_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M},\{p_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}\right), εj∼Gumbel​(0,σ)\varepsilon_{j}\sim\text{Gumbel}(0,\sigma) being independent noise. βj:=βmax​(1−α​j−1d−1),\beta_{j}:=\beta_{\max}\left(1-\alpha\frac{j-1}{d-1}\right),
