G.2 Architectures and Backbone Details

G.2.1 Masked Autoencoder (MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, MiniBooNE)

For image and tabular data, we train a masked autoencoder via self-supervised learning on the full dataset. Given an input xx, a random subset of features is revealed via a binary mask m∈{0,1}dm\in\{0,1\}^{d}, and the model learns an encoder z=fθ​(x⊙m,m)z=f_{\theta}(x\odot m,m) and decoder x^=gθ​(z)\hat{x}=g_{\theta}(z) to reconstruct the full input using an MSE objective. The encoder receives both the masked input and the mask itself, allowing it to distinguish between zero-valued features and unobserved ones. The masking ratio is sampled uniformly during training to expose the model to a wide range of partial observations. After pretraining, the encoder is frozen and used as the representation backbone for echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k. For downstream evaluation, a linear probe is trained on zz for classification under random masking to simulate partial observations; this ensures that the probe is calibrated to the type of partial inputs encountered during sequential acquisition. The same frozen encoder is shared across all baselines and echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k.

G.2.2 TABULA Foundation Model

For single-cell RNA-seq, we use the pretrained TABULA foundation model (Ding et al., 2025), a self-supervised transformer designed for single-cell transcriptomic data. TABULA is trained on large-scale single-cell atlases and can embed partially observed gene expression profiles into cell-level representations. When a subset of genes is unobserved, TABULA treats these entries as missing and produces an embedding conditioned only on the available genes. This native support for partial observations makes it well-suited as a backbone for echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k. The downstream task of cell-type annotation is evaluated via a linear probe trained on top of the cell embeddings. We use TABULA without any fine-tuning; the model weights are frozen throughout both policy learning and evaluation.

G.2.3 VirTues Foundation Model

For the NSCLC patient cohort, we deploy echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with the VirTues spatial proteomics foundation model (Wenckstern et al., 2025). VirTues is a graph-based transformer that operates on cell-level protein expression profiles within tissue sections, producing both cell-level and tissue-level representations. Tissue-level representations are obtained by averaging the cell-level summary tokens across all cells in the tissue sample. When a protein marker is unobserved, its expression value is treated as missing in the cell-level input, and VirTues produces an embedding conditioned on the available markers. Linear probes are trained for cancer subtyping and grading using the tissue-level embeddings. Importantly, the same echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k policy is used for both downstream tasks: the acquisition order is determined once by the policy and then evaluated on both tasks, demonstrating task-agnostic panel design.

G.2.4 GeoSpatial Encoder

For MMEarth-Bench, a masked encoder is used. Concretely, each of the 12 Earth-observation modalities is first converted to a modality-level vector by global average pooling for spatial inputs and identity for tile-level inputs, then projected to a shared dimension and multiplied by a binary modality mask indicating which modalities are observed. The masked per-modality projections are concatenated together with the mask itself and passed through an MLP encoder to produce a latent representation zz. This encoder is trained under random modality masking, so it learns to make reconstructions from arbitrary partial modality subsets while explicitly distinguishing unobserved modalities from zero-valued features.

Backbone-agnosticism.

Across all settings, both echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k and the baselines have access only to the pretrained models during the feature selection phase. Linear probes are used exclusively for downstream evaluation after feature acquisition. echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k interfaces with each backbone only through the partial embedding 𝒛⁡(St)\bm{z}(S_{t}) and the full-information target 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star}; no architecture-specific modifications are needed. This design means that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k can be deployed with any new backbone simply by providing the embedding function, without rewriting any acquisition logic.

G.3 Evaluation Protocol

Each dataset is partitioned into training, validation, and test splits. For image and tabular tasks, we use a 70:15:15 split. For cell-type annotation, we adopt the predefined splits released with TABULA (Ding et al., 2025), and for cancer subtyping and grading, we follow the test splits defined in (Wenckstern et al., 2025).

Acquisition curves.

The primary evaluation metric is the acquisition curve: for each method, we plot downstream performance (MSE or classification accuracy) as a function of the number of features acquired t∈[[1,d]]t\in[\![1,d]\!]. This allows us to compare methods across the full range of acquisition budgets and identify regimes where differences are most pronounced. In practice, the early regime (5–25% of features) is of greatest interest, since this is where cost savings are largest.

Linear probes.

For all real-world datasets, downstream performance is evaluated by training a linear probe on the partial embeddings 𝒛⁡(St)\bm{z}(S_{t}) produced by the frozen backbone. A single linear probe is trained per downstream task using random masking augmentation and held fixed across acquisition budgets. This ensures that the evaluation is task-specific (it depends on the downstream labels) while the acquisition policy remains task-agnostic.

Reproducibility.

All experiments are run with three random seeds for both the echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k policy and the downstream evaluation. The Random baseline is additionally averaged over five independent runs per seed to reduce variance. Error bands in all figures correspond to standard error across seeds.

G.4 Baselines

We compare echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k against a total of 15 baselines spanning synthetic (S), image (I), tabular (T), single-cell RNA-seq (C), and multiplex imaging (M) datasets. Below, we describe each baseline and indicate the settings in which it is evaluated.

G.4.1 Oracle and Random Baselines

Oracle (S, I, T).

A one-step myopic oracle that greedily selects the next feature maximizing the immediate reduction in distance between the current embedding and the full (gold) embedding. This policy is anti-causal: it has access to unobserved features and corresponds to the oracle analyzed in our theoretical results (§3). It serves as an upper bound on greedy acquisition performance but is not deployable at test time.

Random (S, I, T, C, M).

Selects the next view uniformly at random from the set of unobserved features. Provides a minimal reference point for all experiments.

G.4.2 Model-Driven Heuristic Baselines

Prior (S).

Specific to the synthetic setting. Ranks features according to their unconditional expected contribution 𝔼⁡[Ej]\mathbb{E}[E_{j}], which under Assumption 3.2 admits the closed form:

𝔼⁡[𝑬j]=‖𝐰j‖22​Γ​(1−2​σ)​e2​ηj​∑m=1Mpm​e2​βj​zm∝‖𝐰j‖22​e2​ηj​∑m=1Mpm​e2​βj​zm.\mathbb{E}[\bm{E}_{j}]=\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}\Gamma(1-2\sigma)e^{2\eta_{j}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}p_{m}e^{2\beta_{j}z_{m}}\propto\|\mathbf{w}_{j}\|_{2}^{2}e^{2\eta_{j}}\sum_{m=1}^{M}p_{m}e^{2\beta_{j}z_{m}}.

Unlike echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, this baseline does not condition on observed features and therefore captures only population-level feature importance.

GIR (I, T, S, M).

Global Impact Ranking is a practical extension of Prior that does not rely on a known generative model. For each feature ii, a validation-set score si:=‖𝒛full−𝒛−i‖2s_{i}:=\|\bm{z}_{\text{full}}-\bm{z}_{-i}\|_{2} is computed, where 𝒛full\bm{z}_{\mathrm{full}} denotes the self-supervised embedding obtained using all features and 𝒛−i\bm{z}_{-i} denotes the embedding obtained when feature ii is withheld. This induces a fixed, instance-independent acquisition order that captures population-level importance but not individual-level adaptivity.

ESM-Max, ESM-Min (M).

For multiplex imaging only. Protein markers are embedded using ESM2 (Lin et al., 2023). For each marker, pairwise Euclidean distances are computed in the ESM2 embedding space. Markers are ranked by either minimum (ESM-Min) or maximum (ESM-Max) distance, yielding fixed acquisition orders based on semantic similarity or dissimilarity, following (Jain et al., 2025).

G.4.3 Unsupervised Feature Selection Baselines

The following methods were originally designed to identify informative feature subsets given full feature access (Solorio-Fernández et al., 2020). We adapt them to the sequential acquisition setting by using their induced feature rankings as acquisition orders. While not designed for instance-adaptive or sequential settings, they provide strong unsupervised baselines for ranking-based selection. All scores are computed on the validation set and induce a fixed acquisition order applied at test time.

Variance (I, T, S).

Ranks features by their marginal variance over the validation set, selecting in decreasing order of variance.

spec-φ3\varphi_{3} (I, T).

Ranks features based on alignment with the leading k−1k\!-\!1 eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian, where kk is the number of clusters (Zhao and Liu, 2007). Features with stronger alignment to these optimal soft cluster indicators receive higher scores.

Laplacian Score (I, T).

The Laplacian Score (He et al., 2005) evaluates features by how well they preserve local geometric structure encoded by a nearest-neighbor graph. For each feature rr, it computes Lr=f~r⊤​L​f~rf~r⊤​D​f~rL_{r}=\frac{\widetilde{f}_{r}^{\top}L\widetilde{f}_{r}}{\widetilde{f}_{r}^{\top}D\widetilde{f}_{r}}, where L=D−SL=D-S is the graph Laplacian, SS is the similarity matrix, and f~r\widetilde{f}_{r} is the mean-centered weighted feature vector. Features with smaller scores are ranked higher.

MCFS (I, T).

Multi-Cluster Feature Selection (Cai et al., 2010) selects features via spectral analysis of the graph Laplacian. It first solves the generalized eigenvalue problem L​y=λ​D​yLy=\lambda Dy to obtain KK eigenvectors Y=[y1,…,yK]Y=[y_{1},\ldots,y_{K}]. For each yky_{k}, it solves an ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularized regression minak⁡‖yk−XT​ak‖2+β​|ak|\min_{a_{k}}\|y_{k}-X^{T}a_{k}\|^{2}+\beta|a_{k}| to obtain sparse coefficients. Features are ranked by MCFS​(j)=maxk⁡|ak,j|\texttt{MCFS}(j)=\max_{k}|a_{k,j}| and selected in decreasing order.

UDFS (I, T).

Unsupervised Discriminative Feature Selection (Yang et al., 2011) learns a sparse projection matrix W∈ℝd×cW\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times c} by minimizing local discriminative scores with ℓ2,1\ell_{2,1}-norm regularization: minWT​W=I⁡Tr​(WT​M​W)+γ​‖W‖2,1\min_{W^{T}W=I}\text{Tr}(W^{T}MW)+\gamma\|W\|_{2,1}, where MM encodes local neighborhood structure via kk-nearest neighbors. Features are ranked by the row norms ‖wi‖2\|w_{i}\|_{2} of WW in descending order.

SVD-Ent (I, T).

SVD-Entropy (Varshavsky et al., 2006) ranks features by their contribution to SVD-entropy. For each feature ii, its contribution is CEi=E⁡(A)−E⁡(A−i)\text{CE}_{i}=E(A)-E(A_{-i}), where E=−1log⁡N∑j=1NVjlogVjE=-\frac{1}{\log N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}V_{j}\log V_{j} and Vj=sj2/∑ksk2V_{j}=s_{j}^{2}/\sum_{k}s_{k}^{2} are normalized squared singular values. Features with larger CEi\mathrm{CE}_{i} are ranked higher.

G.4.4 Adaptive Label-Free Baselines

The baselines above induce fixed, instance-independent acquisition orders. To compare against policies that condition acquisition on the current instance, we additionally evaluate the following label-free adaptive baselines on MiniBooNE and hPancreas (§ H.3). As for echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, these methods observe only the currently acquired values and the acquisition mask at deployment, and never access the full-view embedding or downstream labels.

GSMRL-AIR (T, C).

An instance-adaptive RL method based on acquisition with generative surrogate models (Li and Oliva, 2021), adapted to the label-free setting. The policy conditions its action selection on the per-sample conditional imputations of unobserved features produced by a generative surrogate, so that acquisition decisions depend on the values observed for each instance.

ALG (T, C).

Adaptive Latent Gain is a learned regressor that predicts, for each unobserved view, the conditional one-step improvement in representation recovery directly from the current partial observation, and greedily acquires the view with the largest predicted gain. ALG shares the reward and state representation of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, but optimizes only the immediate gain rather than a long-horizon objective, and therefore isolates the contribution of sequential planning.

CIG (T).

Cluster Information Gain fits a Gaussian mixture model to the training data and scores each unobserved feature by the mutual information between the feature and the mixture component under the posterior given the currently observed features. The feature with the largest information gain is acquired next. Evaluated on MiniBooNE only.

G.4.5 Summary Table

G.5 Implementation Details of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k

We cast sequential feature acquisition in echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k as a finite-horizon decision problem over partial observations, closely aligned with the conditional surrogate objective analyzed in § 3. The goal of the agent is to sequentially select features so as to minimize the discrepancy between the latent representation induced by the acquired subset and the full-information latent representation of a frozen self-supervised model.

G.5.1 MDP Formulation

Let dd denote the total number of features and TT the acquisition budget. An episode corresponds to sequentially selecting TT features without replacement. At step tt, the agent has observed a subset St⊆{1,…,d}S_{t}\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\}. We define a finite-horizon Markov decision process (𝒮,𝒜,P,r)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},P,r) as follows.

State.

The observable state summarizes the acquisition history and the induced latent representation:

st:=(St,𝒛⁡(St),t/T,‖𝒛⁡(St)‖2,𝒙⊙𝒎t)s_{t}:=\left(S_{t},\bm{z}(S_{t}),t/T,\|\bm{z}(S_{t})\|_{2},\bm{x}\odot\bm{m}_{t}\right)

where 𝒎t∈{0,1}d\bm{m}_{t}\in\{0,1\}^{d} is the binary acquisition mask corresponding to StS_{t}, and 𝒛⁡(St)\bm{z}(S_{t}) denotes the latent embedding produced by the frozen self-supervised encoder given the partially observed input. This state representation renders the process Markov with respect to the surrogate objective.

Action.

At each step, the agent selects a feature index at∈𝒜t:={1,…,d}∖Sta_{t}\in\mathcal{A}_{t}:=\{1,\dots,d\}\setminus S_{t}, corresponding to acquiring a previously unobserved feature. We apply invalid action masking (Huang and Ontañón, 2020), assigning zero probability to actions in StS_{t} during policy evaluation and optimization.

Transition.

Transitions are deterministic: selecting at=ja_{t}=j yields St+1=St∪{j}S_{t+1}=S_{t}\cup\{j\} and updates the latent embedding to 𝒛⁡(St+1)\bm{z}(S_{t+1}).

G.5.2 Reward Design

Let 𝒛∗\bm{z}^{*} denote the latent embedding obtained from the full feature set. Consistent with the surrogate loss analyzed in § 3, we define the instantaneous reward as the normalized reduction in representation error:

rt=(1+1{t<t0}λ)(‖𝒛∗−𝒛⁡(S)‖2−‖𝒛∗−𝒛⁡(S∪{j})‖2‖𝒛∗−𝒛⁡(S0)‖2),r_{t}=(1+\text{1}\{t<t_{0}\}\lambda)\left(\frac{\|\bm{z}^{*}-\bm{z}(S)\|_{2}-\|\bm{z}^{*}-\bm{z}(S\cup\{j\})\|_{2}}{\|\bm{z}^{*}-\bm{z}(S_{0})\|_{2}}\right),

where λ>0\lambda>0 is the gain factor and S0S_{0} denotes the singleton initial feature set. This reward is a shaped version of the marginal gain Δ⁡(at∣St)=‖𝒛∗−𝒛⁡(St)‖2−‖𝒛∗−𝒛⁡(St∪{at})‖2\Delta(a_{t}\mid S_{t})=\|\bm{z}^{*}-\bm{z}(S_{t})\|_{2}-\|\bm{z}^{*}-\bm{z}(S_{t}\cup\{a_{t}\})\|_{2}, which serves as a proxy for the conditional expected contribution 𝔼⁡[Eat∣ℱt]\mathbb{E}[E_{a_{t}}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}] appearing in our theoretical analysis. The step-dependent amplification factor (1+λ1{t<t0})(1+\lambda\text{1}\{t<t_{0}\}) encourages refinement in early acquisition stages, where marginal reductions are typically largest.

G.5.3 Policy Learning

We learn a stochastic policy πθ​(at∣st)\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid s_{t}) using PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) with invalid action masking (Huang and Ontañón, 2020). During both training and inference, the policy has access only to the frozen self-supervised encoder and the induced latent representations. Downstream task labels and linear probes are used exclusively for post-hoc evaluation and do not influence the policy or reward.

G.5.4 Hyperparameters

We implement echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k using the Stable-Baselines3 (SB3) (Raffin et al., 2021) framework with sb3-contrib for support of masked action spaces. Unless mentioned, all PPO parameters are default of SB3. All experiments were conducted on NVIDIA A100 GPUs (80GB) with 128 AMD EPYC 7543 32-core processors. Table 7 summarizes the key hyperparameters across datasets.

The step threshold t0t_{0} is uniformly set to half of the episode length TT. Across experiments, the acquisition budget TT is chosen to lie between 5% and 25% of the total number of available features, depending on the dataset. We set γ=0.98\gamma=0.98 for small-horizon acquisition and γ=0.99\gamma=0.99 for long-horizon (hPancreas). For datasets with fewer features, we train for 300,000 steps; for larger feature spaces, we train for 500,000 steps (except for MMEarth-Bench, where we train for 200,000 steps).

Appendix H Additional Experiments

H.1 Controlled Synthetic Experiment

We first isolate the core question in a controlled setting with known data-generating process: how much does conditioning on partial observations help? For the synthetic data, we consider a randomized isotropic linear regression task with 𝑾∼𝒩⁡(0,1d​𝑰d)\bm{W}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\frac{1}{d}\bm{I}_{d}) and ε′∼Gumbel​(μ′,σ′)\varepsilon^{\prime}\sim\text{Gumbel}(\mu^{\prime},\sigma^{\prime}) yielding labels y=𝑾⊤​𝒙+ε′y=\bm{W}^{\top}\bm{x}+\varepsilon^{\prime}. We fit 𝑾^\widehat{{\bm{W}}} via ridge regression on the full feature set (see Assumption 3.2), with labels from isotropic linear regression (details in § G.1.6). Fig. 6 confirms that the optimal test-time policy consistently outperforms both non-oracle baselines and closely tracks the oracle in early stages, validating the theoretical separation of §3 and motivating the long-horizon RL strategy of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k.

H.2 Extended Baseline Comparisons

In vision and tabular settings, features are individually cheap but collectively redundant; a policy that identifies the most informative subset early reduces measurement overhead at test time. For MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and MiniBooNE, we train a masked autoencoder and freeze the encoder as echo-kk’s backbone. For hPancreas, we use TABULA (Ding et al., 2025) scRNA foundation model. echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k interfaces with it only through 𝒛⁡(⋅)\bm{z}(\cdot) and 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star}, requiring no architecture-specific changes (see § G.2 for backbone details).

Results on MNIST and Fashion-MNIST. Both datasets are downsampled to 14×1414\times 14 following Li and Oliva (2021), yielding d=196d=196 pixel-features with 10-class classification as the downstream task. The goal is to classify each image (handwritten digit or clothing item) by sequentially revealing as few pixels as possible. All methods start from the same top-corner pixel (Fig. 8). echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k rapidly concentrates its acquisitions on discriminative image regions, achieving gains of up to 12% over all non-oracle baselines in the early regime (10–20% of pixels). No single baseline is consistently second-best: Variance leads on MNIST while Random is surprisingly competitive on Fashion-MNIST.

Results on MiniBooNE. MiniBooNE contains d=33d=33 reconstructed physics variables from a neutrino experiment, with binary signal-vs-background classification as the downstream task; these variables are costly to compute and highly correlated (see § G.1). echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k outperforms all heuristic baselines and the one-step oracle (Fig. 7). We attribute this to the oracle’s myopic strategy, which over-selects correlated variables early and suffers diminishing returns, whereas echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k optimizes over a long horizon and learns to exploit complementary information.

H.3 Comparison with Adaptive Acquisition Policies

Most baselines in the main text are fixed acquisition orderings. To verify that the gains of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k are not solely due to comparison against fixed rankings, we compare against label-free controls that condition acquisition on the current instance and match the information setting of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k:

  • •

    GSMRL-AIR, an instance-adaptive RL method that conditions action selection on the per-sample conditional imputations of a generative surrogate (Li and Oliva, 2021), adapted to the label-free setting.

  • •

    Adaptive Latent Gain (ALG), a learned regressor that predicts the conditional one-step representation improvement directly from the current partial observation. ALG shares the reward and state representation of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, but not its long-horizon objective.

  • •

    Cluster Information Gain (CIG), which scores candidate views by mutual information under a fitted Gaussian mixture model posterior (MiniBooNE only).

All methods observe only the currently acquired values and the acquisition mask, and never access the full-view embedding or downstream labels at deployment.

Table 8 shows that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k outperforms all adaptive controls at every budget on both datasets, including GSMRL-AIR, a fully adaptive RL baseline operating under the same label-free constraints. The comparison with ALG is particularly informative: both methods use representation improvement to guide acquisition, but echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k optimizes gains over a longer horizon. This indicates that the advantage of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k comes from long-horizon planning rather than from the recovery signal alone.

H.4 Comparison with Supervised Acquisition

Table 9 reports the full comparison of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with five supervised acquisition methods on MiniBooNE: DIME (Gadgil et al., 2023), GDFS (Covert et al., 2023), SEFA (Norcliffe et al., 2025), GSMRL (Li and Oliva, 2021), and EDDI (Ma et al., 2019). Unlike echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, these methods use downstream labels during policy learning.

At 10% acquisition, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k is within 0.2 points of the best supervised method and exceeds four of the five, despite never observing downstream labels. The gap is largest at 20%, where GDFS leads by 3.0 points, and narrows to 0.9 and 0.5 points at 40% and 60%, respectively. Given that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k never observes downstream labels during training, we view this as the expected cost of task agnosticism.

H.5 Cost of Task Agnosticism

When a single downstream task is fixed and sufficient labels are available, a task-specific policy may be preferable. To quantify this trade-off, we train supervised acquisition policies for NSCLC subtyping (S) and grading (G) using the same architecture and training budget as echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, replacing the latent reward with the downstream-loss improvement

rtsup=ℓ⁡(g⁡(𝒛⁡(𝑷t−1)),y)−ℓ⁡(g⁡(𝒛⁡(𝑷t)),y).r_{t}^{\mathrm{sup}}=\ell\big(g(\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t-1})),y\big)-\ell\big(g(\bm{z}({\bm{P}}_{t})),y\big).

PPO-Subtype and PPO-Grade optimize their respective endpoints, while PPO-Multitask averages the two task-specific losses at each step. We evaluate each policy on both tasks.

At 20% acquisition, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k trails the corresponding task-specific policies by 0.4 points on subtyping and 2.0 points on grading (Table 10). The specialized policies also transfer poorly across endpoints, losing approximately 3–5 points when evaluated on the other task. More importantly, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k is within 0.4, 0.1, and 0.0 points of PPO-Multitask in mean accuracy at 20%, 40%, and 60%, respectively, despite using neither task label. This quantifies the expected cost of task agnosticism, while showing that preserving the pretrained representation nearly matches direct multitask supervision.

H.6 Robustness to Partially Observed Data

Table 11 provides additional robustness results under partially observed reference data on MNIST-14 and FMNIST-14. We train echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k after randomly masking an mm-fraction of views when computing the reference representation used for the self-supervised reward. Across both datasets, performance degrades smoothly as m increases, rather than collapsing. On MNIST-14, partially observed-reference policies remain close to or even slightly above the complete-reference policy across several budgets, indicating that the acquisition policy can tolerate substantial noise in the reference target. On FMNIST-14, the degradation is more visible but remains gradual: even with 50% missing reference views, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k stays competitive with strong baselines and preserves most of its early-budget advantage. These results complement the biological experiments in Table 1, showing that the method’s robustness to incomplete reference data is not specific to a single modality or dataset.

H.7 Heterogeneous Acquisition Costs

To test whether echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k can adapt when views have nonuniform acquisition costs, we run a controlled cost-aware experiment on MNIST-14. We assign each pixel a sample-dependent acquisition cost based on its intensity, rescaled to the range [0.25,2.0][0.25,2.0], so that the policy must trade off representation recovery against cumulative cost. We compare a cost-aware variant of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, trained with a cost-penalized reward and cost information in the state, against the standard cost-unaware policy.

Fig. 8 shows that cost-aware training changes the acquisition behavior. Over the first ten acquisitions, the cost-aware policy selects substantially cheaper pixels on average than the cost-unaware policy, reducing the mean acquisition cost from 0.89 to 0.56. This shift also improves performance in the low-budget regime: when accuracy is plotted against cumulative cost rather than number of pixels, the cost-aware policy reaches high accuracy with fewer cost units. As the budget grows, both policies converge, indicating that cost-awareness is most useful when acquisition resources are limited. This controlled experiment confirms that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k can incorporate heterogeneous costs by changing the reward and state, without modifying the representation-recovery objective.

H.8 Adaptive Stopping

A fixed acquisition horizon may be restrictive in deployment, where the policy should also decide whether the currently acquired views are already sufficient. We extend echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with a STOP action, converting the fixed-horizon MDP into an optimal-stopping problem. For a measurement action aa, the reward is

rt=e⁡(𝑷t−1)−e⁡(𝑷t)e⁡(𝑷0)+ϵ−λ​ca,e⁡(𝑷)=‖𝒛⁡(𝑷)−𝒛⋆‖2,r_{t}=\frac{e({\bm{P}}_{t-1})-e({\bm{P}}_{t})}{e({\bm{P}}_{0})+\epsilon}-\lambda c_{a},\qquad e({\bm{P}})=\|\bm{z}({\bm{P}})-\bm{z}^{\star}\|_{2},

while STOP terminates the episode with zero additional reward. Since STOP yields zero future reward, the policy continues only when the expected cumulative representation gain outweighs the acquisition cost, and with γ=1\gamma=1, the learned stopping time τ\tau directly trades recovery against total acquisition cost. As in echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k, 𝒛⋆\bm{z}^{\star} is used only to construct the label-free training reward; at deployment, both acquisition and stopping depend only on the current partial state.

On MiniBooNE, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k with stopping reaches 86.06% accuracy at a mean of 9.86 acquired features, showing instance-dependent stopping (Table 12). This matches the fixed-horizon policy at a comparable budget (86.11% at t=10t=10), while requiring no budget to be specified in advance. Together with the heterogeneous-cost experiment above, this shows that the representation-recovery objective of echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k can be combined with cost-aware rewards to decide both which views to acquire and when to stop.

H.9 Empirical Validation of the Near Isometry Assumption

A key ingredient in our theoretical analysis is Assumption 3.4 (Near Isometry), which requires that the normalized columns of the embedding weight matrix are approximately orthogonal. We validate this assumption empirically on two classes of models.

H.9.1 DinoV2 Foundation Models

We examine the DINOv2 family of vision transformers (Oquab et al., 2023), including ViT-S/14, ViT-B/14, ViT-L/14, and ViT-G/14 (with register tokens). For each model, we: (1) extract the final MLP projection weights 𝑾∈ℝp×d\bm{W}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times d} from the last transformer block’s feed-forward network (fc2 layer); (2) normalize columns to get 𝑩\bm{B} and compute the Gram matrix 𝑮=𝑩⊤​𝑩\bm{G}=\bm{B}^{\top}\bm{B}; (3) analyze the distribution of the off-diagonal elements of 𝑮−𝑰d\bm{G}-\bm{I}_{d}. As shown in Fig. 9, these values concentrate tightly near zero across all model scales, confirming approximate orthogonality. Larger models exhibit tighter concentration, consistent with theoretical expectations for high-dimensional random-like weight matrices.

H.9.2 Trained Autoencoders

We further validate the assumption on trained autoencoders across varying dimensions dd from 32 to 4096. For each dimension, we generate low-rank data 𝑿⊤=𝑼​𝑽⊤+ϵ\bm{X}^{\top}=\bm{U}\bm{V}^{\top}+\bm{\epsilon} where 𝑼∈ℝn×r\bm{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, 𝑽∈ℝd×r\bm{V}\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times r}. We extract the last layer weight matrix 𝑾\bm{W} and compute the effective rank pe​f​f\text{p}_{eff} using the entropy of normalized singular values (Roy and Vetterli, 2007):

peff=exp(−∑isi∑ksklogsi∑ksk).p_{\text{eff}}=\exp\left(-\sum_{i}\frac{s_{i}}{\sum_{k}s_{k}}\log\frac{s_{i}}{\sum_{k}s_{k}}\right).

We sample random subsets J⊆{1,…,d}J\subseteq\{1,\dots,d\} of varying sizes mm, normalize the corresponding weight vectors to form 𝑩J\bm{B}_{J}, and compute ‖𝑩J⊤​𝑩J−𝑰m‖op\|\bm{B}_{J}^{\top}\bm{B}_{J}-\bm{I}_{m}\|_{\text{op}}. We compare against the theoretical bound C⁡(m/peff+m/peff)C\left(\sqrt{m/p_{\text{eff}}}+m/p_{\text{eff}}\right). Across 50 repetitions, the near isometry property holds with C∈[0.93,1.73]C\in[0.93,1.73] across all tested dimensions. As dd increases, the standard deviation of off-diagonal elements decreases, validating that trained neural network weights naturally form near-orthonormal systems (Fig. 10).

H.10 Analysis of Markers Acquired by echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k on Spatial Proteomics

In Fig. 11, we analyze the distribution of markers chosen by echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k on the NSCLC dataset tasks: cancer subtyping and grading from the marker panel provided by (Cords et al., 2024). In an unsupervised fashion, echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k prioritizes markers that are well-established in the clinical literature for their roles in tumor characterization and microenvironmental context:

  • •

    panCK: a pan-cytokeratin marker for epithelial (tumor) cell identity, consistently selected first.

  • •

    Ki-67: a proliferation marker widely used in clinical grading of lung cancers (Martin et al., 2004).

  • •

    CD4: a marker of helper T-cell infiltration, reflecting the adaptive immune response in the tumor microenvironment.

  • •

    LYVE-1: a marker of lymphatic endothelial cells, relevant to lymphatic involvement and metastatic potential.

This early selection pattern suggests that echo-​k\textsc{echo}\textrm{-}k effectively identifies markers with strong relevance to both tumor biology and immune context, thereby supporting both subtyping and grading tasks without any supervision. The alignment with clinical domain knowledge provides additional validation that the self-supervised acquisition objective captures diagnostically meaningful information.

NeurIPS Paper Checklist

The checklist is designed to encourage best practices for responsible machine learning research, addressing issues of reproducibility, transparency, research ethics, and societal impact. Do not remove the checklist: The papers not including the checklist will be desk rejected. The checklist should follow the references and follow the (optional) supplemental material. The checklist does NOT count towards the page limit.

Please read the checklist guidelines carefully for information on how to answer these questions. For each question in the checklist:

  • •

    You should answer [Yes] , [No] , or [N/A] .

  • •

    [N/A] means either that the question is Not Applicable for that particular paper or the relevant information is Not Available.

  • •

    Please provide a short (1–2 sentence) justification right after your answer (even for [N/A] ).

The checklist answers are an integral part of your paper submission. They are visible to the reviewers, area chairs, senior area chairs, and ethics reviewers. You will also be asked to include it (after eventual revisions) with the final version of your paper, and its final version will be published with the paper.

The reviewers of your paper will be asked to use the checklist as one of the factors in their evaluation. While [Yes] is generally preferable to [No] , it is perfectly acceptable to answer [No] provided a proper justification is given (e.g., error bars are not reported because it would be too computationally expensive” or “we were unable to find the license for the dataset we used”). In general, answering [No] or [N/A] is not grounds for rejection. While the questions are phrased in a binary way, we acknowledge that the true answer is often more nuanced, so please just use your best judgment and write a justification to elaborate. All supporting evidence can appear either in the main paper or the supplemental material, provided in appendix. If you answer [Yes] to a question, in the justification please point to the section(s) where related material for the question can be found.

IMPORTANT, please:

  • •

    Delete this instruction block, but keep the section heading “NeurIPS Paper Checklist",

  • •

    Keep the checklist subsection headings, questions/answers and guidelines below.

  • •

    Do not modify the questions and only use the provided macros for your answers.

  1. 1.

    Claims

  2. Question: Do the main claims made in the abstract and introduction accurately reflect the paper’s contributions and scope?

  3. Answer: [Yes]

  4. Justification: The paper introduces ECHO-kk, provides theoretical justifications, and experiments, as reflected in the abstract and introduction.

  5. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the abstract and introduction do not include the claims made in the paper.

    • •

      The abstract and/or introduction should clearly state the claims made, including the contributions made in the paper and important assumptions and limitations. A [No] or [N/A] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers.

    • •

      The claims made should match theoretical and experimental results, and reflect how much the results can be expected to generalize to other settings.

    • •

      It is fine to include aspirational goals as motivation as long as it is clear that these goals are not attained by the paper.

  6. 2.

    Limitations

  7. Question: Does the paper discuss the limitations of the work performed by the authors?

  8. Answer: [Yes]

  9. Justification: The paper contains an impact and limitations statement in the appendix which discusses the limitations of the work.

  10. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper has no limitation while the answer [No] means that the paper has limitations, but those are not discussed in the paper.

    • •

      The authors are encouraged to create a separate “Limitations” section in their paper.

    • •

      The paper should point out any strong assumptions and how robust the results are to violations of these assumptions (e.g., independence assumptions, noiseless settings, model well-specification, asymptotic approximations only holding locally). The authors should reflect on how these assumptions might be violated in practice and what the implications would be.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the scope of the claims made, e.g., if the approach was only tested on a few datasets or with a few runs. In general, empirical results often depend on implicit assumptions, which should be articulated.

    • •

      The authors should reflect on the factors that influence the performance of the approach. For example, a facial recognition algorithm may perform poorly when image resolution is low or images are taken in low lighting. Or a speech-to-text system might not be used reliably to provide closed captions for online lectures because it fails to handle technical jargon.

    • •

      The authors should discuss the computational efficiency of the proposed algorithms and how they scale with dataset size.

    • •

      If applicable, the authors should discuss possible limitations of their approach to address problems of privacy and fairness.

    • •

      While the authors might fear that complete honesty about limitations might be used by reviewers as grounds for rejection, a worse outcome might be that reviewers discover limitations that aren’t acknowledged in the paper. The authors should use their best judgment and recognize that individual actions in favor of transparency play an important role in developing norms that preserve the integrity of the community. Reviewers will be specifically instructed to not penalize honesty concerning limitations.

  11. 3.

    Theory assumptions and proofs

  12. Question: For each theoretical result, does the paper provide the full set of assumptions and a complete (and correct) proof?

  13. Answer: [Yes]

  14. Justification: The paper provides a central theorem bridging the oracle-test-time-policy gap and assumptions in the main, along with detailed proof in the Appendix.

  15. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include theoretical results.

    • •

      All the theorems, formulas, and proofs in the paper should be numbered and cross-referenced.

    • •

      All assumptions should be clearly stated or referenced in the statement of any theorems.

    • •

      The proofs can either appear in the main paper or the supplemental material, but if they appear in the supplemental material, the authors are encouraged to provide a short proof sketch to provide intuition.

    • •

      Inversely, any informal proof provided in the core of the paper should be complemented by formal proofs provided in appendix or supplemental material.

    • •

      Theorems and Lemmas that the proof relies upon should be properly referenced.

  16. 4.

    Experimental result reproducibility

  17. Question: Does the paper fully disclose all the information needed to reproduce the main experimental results of the paper to the extent that it affects the main claims and/or conclusions of the paper (regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not)?

  18. Answer: [Yes]

  19. Justification: The paper provides all experimental details, evaluation protocols, hyperparameters, hardware architecture, and Python libraries.

  20. Guidelines:

    • •

      The answer [N/A] means that the paper does not include experiments.

    • •

      If the paper includes experiments, a [No] answer to this question will not be perceived well by the reviewers: Making the paper reproducible is important, regardless of whether the code and data are provided or not.

    • •

      If the contribution is a dataset and/or model, the authors should describe the steps taken to make their results reproducible or verifiable.

    • •

      Depending on the contribution, reproducibility can be accomplished in various ways. For example, if the contribution is a novel architecture, describing the architecture fully might suffice, or if the contribution is a specific model and empirical evaluation, it may be necessary to either make it possible for others to replicate the model with the same dataset, or provide access to the model. In general. releasing code and data is often one good way to accomplish this, but reproducibility can also be provided via detailed instructions for how to replicate the results, access to a hosted model (e.g., in the case of a large language model), releasing of a model checkpoint, or other means that are appropriate to the research performed.

    • •

      While NeurIPS does not require releasing code, the conference does require all submissions to provide some reasonable avenue for reproducibility, which may depend on the nature of the contribution. For example

      1. (a)

        If the contribution is primarily a new algorithm, the paper should make it clear how to reproduce that algorithm.

      2. (b)

        If the contribution is primarily a new model architecture, the paper should describe the architecture clearly and fully.

      3. (c)

        If the contribution is a new model (e.g., a large language model), then there should either be a way to access this model for reproducing the results or a way to reproduce the model (e.g., with an open-source dataset or instructions for how to construct the dataset).

      4. (d)

        We recognize that reproducibility may be tricky in some cases, in which case authors are welcome to describe the particular way they provide for reproducibility. In the case of closed-source models, it may be that access to the model is limited in some way (e.g., to registered users), but it should be possible for other researchers to have some path to reproducing or verifying the results.

      The instructions should contain the exact command and environment needed to run to reproduce the results. See the NeurIPS code and data submission guidelines (https://neurips.cc/public/guides/CodeSubmissionPolicy) for more details.

      Including this information in the supplemental material is fine, but if the main contribution of the paper involves human subjects, then as much detail as possible should be included in the main paper.

    • •

      According to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics, workers involved in data collection, curation, or other labor should be paid at least the minimum wage in the country of the data collector.

  71. 15.

    Institutional review board (IRB) approvals or equivalent for research with human subjects

      Depending on the country in which research is conducted, IRB approval (or equivalent) may be required for any human subjects research. If you obtained IRB approval, you should clearly state this in the paper.

    • •

      We recognize that the procedures for this may vary significantly between institutions and locations, and we expect authors to adhere to the NeurIPS Code of Ethics and the guidelines for their institution.

      For initial submissions, do not include any information that would break anonymity (if applicable), such as the institution conducting the review.
